Fragmenta ex commentariis in epistulam i ad Corinthios
1 I Cor. i 2
[τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ τῇ οὔσῃ ἐν Κορίνθῳ, ἡγιασμένοις ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, κλητοῖς
ἁγίοις, σὺν πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐπικαλουμένοις τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐν
παντὶ τόπῳ αὐτῶν καὶ ἡμῶν.] [Ὠριγένους] Εἰ πάντες ἦσαν ἐκκλησία, τίς ἔτι χρεία
προ<σ>κεῖσθαι σὺν πᾶσι τοῖς ἐπι καλουμένοις; εἰ πάντες ὁμοίως ἐπεκαλοῦντο, τίς
χρεία μὴ πᾶσιν ἐπικαλουμέ νοις γεγράφθαι μόνον ἀλλὰ πέρ<α> αὐτῶν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ
τοῦ θεοῦ; παρεστήσαμεν ὡς μόνους τοὺς ἐπαινετοὺς χρηματίζειν ἐκκλησίαν
ὀφείλοντας, τοὺς δὲ ψεκτοὺς οὐκ ἀποστάτας μὲν ἔτι παλαίοντας τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀλλ'
<ἔτι> ἐπικαλουμένους, οὐ μὴν ἤδη καὶ ἐκκλησία<ν>. σπεύσωμεν οὖν ἀπὸ τοῦ
ἐπικαλεῖσθαι εἰς τὸ ἀναβῆναι ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τὴν ἄσπιλον καὶ ἄμωμον. 2 i 4–10
[Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τῇ χάριτι τοῦ θεοῦ τῇ δοθείσῃ ὑμῖν ἐν
Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὅτι ἐν παντὶ ἐπλουτίσθητε ἐν αὐτῷ, ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ πάσῃ γνώσει,
καθὼς τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ χριστοῦ ἐβεβαιώθη ἐν ὑμῖν, ὥστε ὑμᾶς μὴ ὑστερεῖσθαι ἐν
μηδενὶ χαρίσματι, ἀπεκδεχομένους τὴν ἀποκά λυψιν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ
Χριστοῦ· ὃς καὶ βεβαιώσει ὑμᾶς ἕως τέλους ἀνεγκλήτους ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου
ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ [Χριστοῦ]. πιστὸς ὁ θεὸς δι' οὗ ἐκλήθητε εἰς κοινωνίαν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ
Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν. παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοί, διὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ
κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἵνα τὸ αὐτὸ λέγητε πάντες, καὶ μὴ ᾖ ἐν ὑμῖν σχίσματα,
ἦτε δὲ κατηρτισμένοι ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ νοῒ καὶ ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ γνώμῃ.] [Ὠριγένους] Οὔτε
ταῦτα ἁμαρτωλοῖς ἁρμόζει οὔτε ἐκεῖνα δικαίοις, φημὶ δὴ τὸ Παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς,
ἀδελφοί, διὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἵνα πάντες τὰ αὐτὰ
λέγητε καὶ μὴ ᾖ ἐν ὑμῖν σχίσματα καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα. ἦν οὖν ἡ ἐκκλησία ἀναμεμιγμένη,
εἴ γε χρὴ ἐκκλησίαν ὀνομάζειν τὸ ὅλον τοῦτο τὸ μικτὸν ἐκ δικαίων καὶ ἀδίκων.
πλὴν οἱ συναγόμενοι ἦσαν ἀναμεμιγμένοι· διὰ τοῦτο μέλλων ὁ ἀπόστολος ἐπὶ ταῖς
ἁμαρτίαις τοὺς συναγομένους μετὰ κακίας ἐλέγχειν, ἀναγκαί<ως> πρῶτον τοὺς
ἐπαίνους ποιεῖται τῶν καλῶς υνερχομένων ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό. Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ μου
πάντοτε· ἄξιον εὐχαριστεῖν ἐφ' οἷς λέγει ἐπαινετοῖς, καὶ οὐ ποτὲ μὲν εὐχαριστεῖν
ποτὲ δὲ μή, ἀλλὰ πάντοτε εὐχαριστεῖν. ἐάν τινα ἴδω ποτὲ μὲν εὖ πράττοντα ποτὲ δὲ
ἁμαρτάνοντα, εὐχαριστῶ περὶ αὐτοῦ οὐ πάντοτε, ἀλλ' ὅτε εὖ ποιεῖ· οὕτω καὶ περὶ
ἐμαυτοῦ. ἐν τίνι δὲ εὐχαριστήσει ὁ εὐχαριστῶν Παῦλος; ἐπὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀκροαταῖς ὧν
γέγονε κατὰ θεὸν πατήρ. ὥσπερ οὖν πατὴρ ἐπὶ υἱοῖς εὐχαριστεῖ ὅτ' ἂν ὑγιαίνωσιν,
ὅτ' ἂν εὖ πράττωσι, τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ὅτ' ἂν βλέπῃ διδάσκαλος τοὺς ἀκροατὰς
ζέοντα τῶι πνεύματι, πλουτοῦντας λόγῳ οφία< >, ἀξίους τοῦ ἐπαινεῖσθαι,
εὐχαριστεῖ πάντοτε περὶ αὐτῶν. Ἴδωμεν οὖν τὴν Χάριν τῶν ἐπαινετῶν ἐν Κορίνθῳ
ἵνα ζηλώσωμεν. Ὅτι ἐν παντὶ ἐπλουτίσθητε ἐν αὐτῷ. μακάριοι οἱ ἐν παντὶ
πλουτοῦντες καὶ μηδενὸς τῶν κατὰ θεὸν ὑστερούμενοι, ἀλλὰ πᾶσαν ἐπιτηδεύοντες
ἀρετὴν καὶ τῶν παρ' αὐτοῦ ἀφθόνως καὶ πλουσίως ἀπολαύοντες δωρεῶν ἐν παντὶ
λόγῳ καὶ πάσῃ γνώσει· ὥστε εἰς μηδεμίαν γραφὴν ἀπορεῖν ἀλλὰ πανταχοῦ ζητεῖν
καὶ εὑρί κειν, καὶ ὅτε δεῖ ἐξηγήσασθαι γραφὴν παντὶ λόγῳ κεχρῆσθαι τῷ τε
διεξοδικῷ καλου μένῳ καὶ τῷ κατὰ ἐρώτησίν τε καὶ ἀπόκρισιν, καὶ παρεσκευάσθαι
λέγειν καὶ κατὰ πάσης αἱρέσεως, καὶ τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας συνίστασθαι δόγματι, καὶ
ἀναπλη ρῶσαι τὸ εἰρημένον ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀποστόλου Ἕτοιμοι ἀεὶ πρὸ ἀπολογίαν παντὶ
τῷ ἀπαιτοῦντι ὑμᾶ λόγον περὶ τῆ ἐν ὑμῖν πί τεω . οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸ ἐν πάσῃ γνώσει·
οὐ μόνον κατὰ τὰς γραφάς, ἀλλ' ἵνα καὶ εἴπῃ· Αὐτὸ γάρ μοι ἔδωκεν τῶν ὄντων τὴν
γνῶ ιν ἀψευδῆ καὶ τὰ τούτοις ἀκόλουθα. ὅτι ἡ γνῶσις τὸ εἰδέναι μόνον ἐμφαίνει, ὁ
δὲ λόγος καὶ τὸ ἐγνωσμένον ἑρμηνεύει. καθὼς τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ χριστοῦ ἐβεβαιώθη
english: Fragments from the commentaries on the First Letter to the Corinthians. On 1 Corinthians 1:2: “to the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, together with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, theirs and ours.” Origen says: if everyone were already the church, what need would there still be to add “together with all who call upon”? And if all alike were calling upon the Name, what need would there be for the letter not to be written only to all who call upon it, but beyond them also to the church of God? We have already shown that only those who deserve praise ought to be styled “church,” while those who deserve blame are not yet apostates—they are still wrestling with sin—but are still calling upon him, and are not yet the church itself. So let us hurry on from mere calling upon him to rising up into the church that is spotless and without blemish.

On 1 Corinthians 1:4–10: “I thank my God always concerning you for the grace of God given you in Christ Jesus, that in everything you were enriched in him, in every word and all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed among you, so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also confirm you to the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord. I appeal to you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be fitted together in the same mind and the same judgment.” Origen says: neither do these praises suit sinners, nor do those rebukes suit the righteous alone—I mean the words “I appeal to you, brothers… that you all say the same things and that there be no divisions among you,” and whatever is like them. So the church was mixed, if one may even call “church” this whole blend of just and unjust. Still, those who were gathering were mixed; therefore, when the apostle was about to convict the gathering for sins done with wickedness, he first, of necessity, offers praise for those who come together well upon the same thing.

“I thank my God always”: it is right to give thanks over the praiseworthy things he names, and not sometimes to thank and sometimes not, but always to thank. If I see someone sometimes doing well and sometimes sinning, I do not thank God concerning him always, but when he does well—and so also concerning myself. In whom, then, does the thanksgiving Paul offer find its ground? In his own hearers, of whom he has become a father according to God. Just as a father gives thanks over sons when they are healthy and when they prosper, so too, whenever a teacher sees his hearers boiling with the Spirit, rich in word and wisdom, worthy of praise, he thanks God always concerning them. Let us look, then, at the grace of those praised in Corinth, so that we may be eager for it.

“That in everything you were enriched in him.” Blessed are those who are rich in everything and lack nothing that belongs to God, but practice every virtue and enjoy his gifts freely and richly—in every word and in all knowledge—so that they are at a loss over no Scripture, but seek and find everywhere; and when a text must be explained they can use every kind of discourse, both the so called continuous exposition and question and answer, and are ready to speak against every heresy, to stand with the dogma of the truth, and to fulfill what the apostle said: “Always ready to make a defense to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you.” So also “in all knowledge”: not only according to the Scriptures, but so that one may say, “For he himself gave me unfailing knowledge of the things that are,” and what follows from that. For knowledge shows knowing alone, while word also interprets what is known. “Just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed”

english: among you. Christ is, if I may put it this way, the chief martyr; and though there are many witnesses to Christ through their death, he is the ruler of the martyrs. This testimony of Christ is firm in some, and in others it is not firm but shaken. For if faith about the testimony is such that from a true disposition one can say, “I am persuaded that neither death nor life” and what follows “will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord,” then the testimony is firm in such a person; but if we are not like that, and are shaken by what happens, the testimony of Christ has not yet been confirmed in us. And again we may take the saying another way: every Scripture that bears witness about Christ is a testimony of Christ; so it is good to be confirmed also in the testimony of Christ that comes from the Scriptures. And otherwise: look at the testimony of Christ—signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will also bore witness with him; and the testimony of Christ is firm in the saints.

“So that you are not lacking in any gift”: as there are many gifts, he will discuss them also later in the letter. “Awaiting the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ”: the righteous person does not have his hopes in this age, but while suffering and facing danger he awaits the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, what Christ Jesus reveals. “Who will also confirm you to the end”: who confirms? Christ Jesus, the Word, Wisdom; and the testimony that is being confirmed is not for a few days, but to the end. “Blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ”: until we arrive there, we do not yet have blamelessness; for we do not know what the coming day will bring forth, and even if someone seems to have blamelessness for the present, it is in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

On 1 Corinthians 1:9: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.” Origen: keep believing him always; for you were called so that we might simply be under Jesus. Great is what God grants the saints: we were called into fellowship with his Son; therefore heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. On 1 Corinthians 1:10: “and that there be no divisions among you.” Origen: the one who agrees in everything with the right word and the church’s dogma concerning Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and further concerning the economy that touches us, concerning resurrection and judgment, and who also follows the church’s canons, is not in a schism.

On 1 Corinthians 1:14, 17: “I thank God that I baptized none of you… for Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of word, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.” Origen: preaching the gospel is greater than baptizing; and because Paul knew that some were set apart for baptizing, he thanks God for having a better lot than baptizing. In Acts the apostles’ works appear: Philip baptized, but Philip did not minister the Spirit to the baptized; rather Peter laid hands on those Philip baptized, and the Spirit came upon them. Philip baptized with water those being born again of water and Holy Spirit, and Peter with the Spirit. Origen again: there is need not so much of word as of power; therefore it is written, “The Lord will give a word to those who preach good news with great power,” the King of the powers of the Beloved. So Christ sent me not to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of word, not in clarity of diction; for if I do that and want to hand on the word that way, the power of Christ does not reach the soul of the hearers, and I empty and tear down the grace of the power.

On 1 Corinthians 1:18: “For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” Origen: the name of the cross seems a scandal; but if someone lends his ears to the word of God and to grace, he will see that this too is a great mystery. Even the pagans have handed down that often, when great plagues or floods or droughts came, these ceased when a person gave himself up for the common good. Why then is it surprising if, when the whole world was sick with error, one had to die for the true plague—to destroy the plague of ignorance and darkness and ruin? And who was able to take this on? Not a prophet, not an apostle, nor any other righteous person; but a divine power had to come down from heaven

english: able to take on dying for all, with a kind of public display, so that through that death a trophy might be raised against the devil. For those who triumph in the world are accustomed to set up trophies against the conquered in the manner of a cross. So the cross of Christ is a trophy against Satan; therefore he says, “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross”—for the one who has come to know what the power of the cross is: that I was freed from evils through that One who died to rescue me from death—“except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.” It is a great good that the world has been crucified to me; through what did this good come to me? Through the cross of Christ. It is a great good for me to be crucified to the world; for if I died to the world, I have been crucified to the world with Christ; but if I live in sins, I have not yet been counted worthy of the good that belongs to the cross. At the same time let us also prepare for trials and for martyrdoms, knowing that whoever denies him has no salvation.

On 1 Corinthians 1:19–21: “For it is written, ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will set aside.’ Where is the wise? Where the scribe? Where the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased through the folly of the preaching to save those who believe.” Origen: it is not the same to be wise and to be wise in this age; for without such an addition the word covers true wisdom. You will understand folly likewise: it is not the same to be a fool and to be a fool in this age; for without the addition “in this age” one is truly a fool. We who believe the words of wisdom are therefore commanded to become fools in this age; for so we seem to people when we believe in Christ Jesus crucified, and believe the resurrection of bodies, and believe that we shall live—not only that those now on earth will later be in the heavens, but that if we sin we shall be handed over to eternal fire. Such we seem to people…

On 1 Corinthians 1:23–31: “but we preach Christ crucified, a scandal to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God… For consider your calling, brothers, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many of noble birth; but God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and God chose the of low birth of the world and the despised, and the things that are not, to abolish the things that are, so that no flesh may boast before God. And from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.’” Origen: we received power from believing in Jesus Christ crucified; and as far as we fall short in that faith, so far we fall short in the power of having in ourselves the things that come from God. And if you want to understand “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and set aside the discernment of the discerning,” picture for me someone very formidable in heretical arguments—say Marcion or Basilides—who seeks with such force for the heretical case that not just anyone can stand against him; then picture someone competent according to the truth, whom God also made competent as a minister of a new covenant, showing all those things to be folly on which the deceived man relied. So he destroys their wisdom—not that of the truly wise, Isaiah, Jeremiah, or Solomon; he destroys seeming wisdom, not the true. And how “in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom”? The wisdom of God is in law and prophets; the world did not know Christ preached in law and prophets. Therefore at the end of the ages he sent Jesus Christ to be crucified for the human race, so that by the folly of the preaching those who believed in Jesus Christ crucified might believe. And he added “according to the flesh” to “not many wise,” knowing there are differences among the wise: some wise according to flesh, some according to spirit; and wise according to flesh are those who have practiced only little phrases and dress up whatever is not truth as if it were truth

english: —what is not truth. Yet even so he did not shut the wise according to flesh out of the faith; for he did not say “No one wise according to the flesh comes to the word,” but that they are exceedingly few. Powerful according to the flesh are those who hold the offices; according to the Spirit you will understand if you see how the Savior was not powerful according to the flesh—he was handed over and crucified from weakness—yet was powerful according to the Spirit, healing every disease and every illness in the people. So look at the apostles: how they were powerful according to the Spirit. One is powerful according to the Spirit also who lives according to the Spirit and by the Spirit puts to death the deeds of the body. Likewise with the of noble birth: of noble birth according to the flesh are those from rich and famous fathers; according to the Spirit the of noble birth are the sons of God, of whom it is written, “As many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God.” Whom then did God choose? Not simply the foolish, but with the addition “of the world”: we who believe are fools as far as the world is concerned. So they laugh and call us fools: “Christians say there is a resurrection of the dead, and that we live after death, and that Jesus whom the Jews crucified was born of a virgin,” and such things. Let them laugh and call us fools; for the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit—they are folly to him. So God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise—not simply the wise, but, by common construction, of the world: God chose the world’s foolish to shame the world’s wise; for truly the world’s wise are put to shame when they worship idols while the unlettered and simple die rather than commit idolatry.

“And God chose the of low birth of the world and the despised”—again with the addition “of the world.” For what is nobler than a soul that leaves the idols and says, “Our fathers acquired false idols, and there is none among them who brings rain”? So God chose the of low birth of the world but of noble birth of God; only let us succeed so that we are not despised before God, of whom it is written that the one who does evil is despised before him. “And the things that are not, to abolish the things that are”: he named “things that are not” the foolish, weak, of low birth, and despised of the world; “things that are,” the of noble birth of the world—for in the world they are somebody, and we are not, worn down by all and despised. Now God chose the things that are not to abolish the things that are, so that no flesh may boast and say, “I was chosen because I am of noble birth.” “And from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption”: for this reason Christ is all these for us, so that what is written may come to pass—“Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” For if the one who boasts in wisdom ought to boast, and Christ is the wisdom, clearly the one who boasts in Christ boasts; and likewise for the rest—I mean sanctification and righteousness.

On 1 Corinthians 2:4–7: “and my word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of Spirit and power, so that your faith might not be in human wisdom but in the power of God. Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect—wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age who are being abolished. But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” Origen: lest someone say, “Then, since he brought the proofs of faith in power and in Spirit, he had no wisdom at all, but the mystery of piety is only to believe, and there is no promise of wisdom in it,” he adds, “Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect—wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age who are being abolished.” For it is one thing to lead people into the faith, and another to unveil the wisdom of God. At the same time he has made clear that the lessons circulating among others are not, in their origin, of humans but of invisible powers that are being abolished. And I would say that the poetic wisdom is of this age, and perhaps rhetoric too; and so is the wisdom that claims to speak about heaven and earth and the administration of the whole. So if we speak wisdom and say it among the perfect, we do not mean the wisdom of this age; for it is not through poems or through any such art. Origen: but we speak wisdom in a mystery—things unknown to the rulers of this age who work the wisdom of the wise of this world; and thus they did not know: they plotted against our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ and crucified him; for if they had known they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Therefore wisdom must also be sought in the word—but after faith, after the way of life, according to what is written: “Desire wisdom; keep the commandments.”

On 1 Corinthians 2:9–11: “But as it is written, ‘What eye has not seen and ear has not heard and has not risen upon a human heart—what God prepared for those who love him.’ But to us God revealed them through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. For who among humans knows the things of a human except the spirit of the human that is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.” Origen: Scripture knows a difference between those who love God and those who fear God, and knows that those who love far surpass those who fear. Some things have been prepared also for those who fear; yet he prepared something greater for those who love than what was prepared for those who fear. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. There is a Spirit that can search everything; the human soul cannot search everything, but a better Spirit had to come to be in us, so that when that Spirit is in us searching everything—even the depths of God—and is mingled with us, we may search together with it everything and the depths of God.

On 1 Corinthians 2:12–15: “Now we have not received the spirit of the world but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may know the things freely given us by God; which things we also speak not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. english: Spirit is to be understood from the apostolic words: “comparing spiritual things with spiritual”—by examining this wording with that wording and gathering like with like, the mind of Scripture is uncovered as it were. In this way I understand the things of God and become taught by the Spirit: not only by having learned the things of the Spirit that moved Isaiah, but also by having the same Spirit that shut and sealed Isaiah’s words; for unless the Spirit opens the prophets’ words, what is shut cannot be opened. And since he said these things, he necessarily adds that there are some people who do not receive the things of the Spirit of God—not because of nature, as the heterodox suppose, but because they have not prepared themselves. For the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit—he was soulish; but when he inclined toward piety and received the Spirit, he became spiritual. And the soulish cannot know that he is examined spiritually; therefore he does not know, about what he hears, that it is examined spiritually; and when the power is tested it convicts the fool—as when I speak taught by the Spirit and speak with power, and the hearer testing the power thinks otherwise and does not assent: the power being tested convicts the fool. And it is not so much that he has rejected what is said as that what is said has rejected him; for “wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, nor dwell in a body in debt to sin.” “The spiritual person examines all things, yet he himself is examined by no one.” The one who no longer walks according to flesh but according to Spirit, and always by care grows it and kindles more the gift of God, prepares for himself to become spiritual; and having become so he is able to examine all things—the Greeks’, the barbarians’, the wise’, the senseless’; and no one can examine him because of the greatness of his understanding and of his reasonings. And if you want to recognize the spiritual person, “by their fruits you will know them.” What then are the fruits of the Spirit by which one must know who is spiritual? Hear the apostle: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self control”; where these are, there is the Spirit, and that one is spiritual; and where any of these is missing, that one is not yet spiritual.

On 1 Corinthians 3:1–3a: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people but as to fleshly, as to infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able; but neither are you able even now.” Origen: of hearers some are perfect—the spiritual, of whom we were also speaking earlier; and those who are not spiritual yet believe in Christ are, as the apostle says, infants in Christ and fleshly in Christ—for I hear “in Christ” as common to both. So those not yet more perfect and not yet exercised in the sacred Scriptures need lesser lessons, which the apostle named milk: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, but neither are you able even now.” And I think there is a scale among spiritual foods: milk, food, true food, solid food, flesh of the Word, and spiritual vegetable. And I dare to say this persuaded by the Scriptures; for he did not say every spiritual food is true food when he says, “My flesh is true food.” What then is not solid food? The more ethical teachings and whatever among ethical matters is weaker—said by way of concession, not by command, stewarded because of the hearers’ weakness. But whatever more perfect teaching among ethical matters belongs to eager and hardworking hearers—these I would call solid food among ethical teachings: teaching about perfect chastity, about virginity or temperance, about martyrdom; these are solid food. english: letter when he says, “Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk”; and in Hebrews also, “You have become ones who need milk and not solid food; for everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant; but solid food is for the perfect, who because of habit have their senses exercised toward distinguishing good and evil.”

On 1 Corinthians 3:3–5: “For where there is jealousy and strife and divisions among you, are you not fleshly and walking according to a human? For whenever someone says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollos,’ are you not humans?” Origen: among human sins the lesser ones are jealousy and strife. If someone is in fornication, such a person is no longer fleshly but worse than fleshly. What then would such a one be? Let us see. I think there is a difference between fleshly and earthy: “As we bore the image of the earthy,” he says, “let us also bear the image of the heavenly.” So if you sin unto death, you are not fleshly but earthy; but if you sin, yet not unto death, you are not wholly earthy nor fallen away from the grace of Christ, but then you are fleshly. And of our walks, one is according to a human, another according to God. If we walk as most humans do, we walk according to a human; but if according to “Let your light shine before humans,” we differ from the many and do not walk according to a human. So the life is clear to the one who can see what is according to a human and what according to God. For whenever someone says, “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” “I am of Cephas”—let us also attend to these. We shall see that sometimes we are not even humans but worse than humans. For the one who then said “I am of Apollos” was speaking of a learned and holy and blessed man; the one who said “I am of Paul,” of a sacred and blessed apostle. But sometimes leanings arise not like the leaning toward Paul or Apollos, but someone leans toward a sinner and sometimes toward a heterodox person. So if those are humans and walk according to flesh who say “I am of Apollos” and “I of Paul,” whenever you say you belong to someone lesser, clearly you are no longer even a human but worse than human; and perhaps it will be said to you, “Brood of vipers.”

On 1 Corinthians 3:6–8: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth; so neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth… and each will receive his own wage according to his own labor.” Origen: if Paul planted, he planted together with God who plants first of all; if Apollos watered, he watered together with Christ who waters first of all; for God plants—therefore it is written, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted,” and again, “My Father is the farmer.” So let us bear fruit lest we be cut down like the barren fig tree. For every tree not producing good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Let us take care that it not be said of us, “I waited for it to produce grapes, and it produced thorns.” For if he says these things about us, he will also say what follows: “And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will remove its hedge and it shall be for plunder, and I will tear down its wall and it shall be for trampling.”

On 1 Corinthians 3:9–15: “For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building. According to the grace of God given me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds upon it. Let each watch how he builds; for no one can lay another foundation besides the one laid, which is Jesus Christ. If anyone builds on this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become clear, for the day will disclose it, because it is revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each has. If anyone’s work remains which he built, he will receive a wage; if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, yet he himself will be saved, but so as through fire.” Origen: since we are not only a field but also God’s building, I seek the master builder of the building and those who work with him. Understanding this the apostle says, “According to the grace given me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation”; for Paul established the church in Corinth that before the apostle was in no way present. english: builds upon it, that one is not the master builder of the church but builds upon the church. So if you want to see that Paul is a wise master builder, hear him: “From Jerusalem and as far as Illyricum I have fulfilled the gospel of God, making it my ambition to preach the gospel not where Christ was named, so that I might not build upon another’s foundation.” And he not only laid a foundation as a wise master builder, but also wrote, as it were, architectural books—how the master builder must build a house, what sort the overseer must be, and elders and deacons and the rest of the church’s fullness; for all these were as it were architectural laws. “So another builds upon it,” he says; “let each watch how he builds.” For this also speaks to me, so that I may not build carelessly, knowing that the work I build—what sort it is—the fire itself will test on that day. And I take care lest, building, I build wood, hay, straw. For if I bring worthless souls uncritically into the church, I have brought to the good foundation Christ Jesus wood, and others hay, and others straw; just as again, if some shine out from the building, and shine so much that some are found analogous to what is written about Jerusalem and the temple—chosen stones and crystal stone and sapphire stones and whatever stones are named there—clearly I have built precious stones upon the foundation. And since God’s temple and building must also have gold, as the temple Solomon built is a symbol of a temple having much gold and silver, if another comes being built up and is found more precious than silver, he would be gold. But I fear lest through me wood and hay and straw enter, and wretched I (even if otherwise judged worthy of salvation—since it is written, “yet he himself will be saved, but so as through fire”) be saved in this way as one who became a cause, by not holding the grace nor building well, of filling the building with wood, hay, straw, which the word of God does not want; for the fire will test what sort each one’s work is.

I want also to take another way the saying, “For no one can lay another foundation besides the one laid, which is Jesus Christ,” and what follows. From the time my Lord Jesus Christ sojourned, this foundation has been preached into the world; and the apostles laid this foundation in Judea, and among the nations the apostle of the nations and his fellow worker Barnabas—“for they gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we to the nations and they to the circumcision.” So once Jesus Christ the Word of God has been preached and this foundation laid, no one can lay another foundation besides Jesus Christ; and those who build upon it, if they are orthodox through everlasting doctrines and divine thoughts and good words and holy deeds, build upon the foundation gold, silver, precious stone. For gold has often been kept, taken for mind and thoughts; if I speak well, I build silver; if I interpret as I ought and urge hearers well toward a way of life, I build precious stones. Yet as many of those who teach Jesus Christ have missed the truth, they have built upon the foundation wood, hay, straw; and I would say that of those from the heresies the more blasphemous are wood, those who sinned less in teaching are hay, and those with thin and, so to speak, lesser faults are straw.

Come, let us also see it according to the letter. What will be said touches each of us; each of us, having received the word of the gospel, received Jesus Christ as foundation, so that in all he does and says and thinks he may build upon this foundation. So if we think and intend good things, we build gold; if speaking purely we say every word spoken in a holy way, we build as silver; if every deed we do is good, we build as precious stone—and God judges the worth and quality of the stones. 1 Cor. 3:16–20: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone ruins God’s temple, God will ruin him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple. Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, ‘He catches the wise in their craftiness,’ and again, ‘The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.’”

Origen says: If you want to learn what the true temple of God is, seek living stones, cleanly quarried, set in place by the Word, standing four-square, with nothing unstable or rolling. For even if holy stones roll on the earth, the stonecutters do not let them keep rolling to the end. So you, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

And with the Apostle it is said that all of us are one temple, each of us a stone of the temple. So he speaks in Ephesians: “So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow-citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling of God in the Spirit.”

So no stone must be ill-fitted to the building. For if two of you agree on earth about any matter they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven—how much more, then, if all the stones agree in one harmony and all share one heart and one soul, will their prayer be able and strong? It is good, then, that we all say the same thing, that we may be fitted together in the same mind and the same judgment; for so you are a building fitted together into a holy temple in the Lord.

And in another sense each of us can be a temple by himself. For if a temple is what has God’s glory, everyone who has God’s glory in himself is in that respect God’s temple. One has more glory or less who makes the name of the Father in heaven glorified by his deeds; therefore it is written, “Those who glorify me I will glorify.” Then we will most of all be God’s temple if we prepare ourselves to receive the Spirit of God. Yet no one who has a spirit of some sin can be God’s temple, because the Spirit of God alone dwells where he judges it right to dwell.

“If anyone ruins God’s temple, God will ruin him.” As far as each person can, even if he is a stone, he ruins God’s temple when he sins; and anyone who puts a stumbling-block before the church also ruins God’s temple. Still more properly the one who fornicates ruins God’s temple, since your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God. So the pure person is called uncorrupted, and the one who is no longer a virgin is called corrupted—as if this deed alone were the corrupting. If, then, this is a work of corruption, let us guard against it above all; for the Lord also, with all who love God, is in incorruption.

So much for that stretch on its own. But because the Corinthians were proud of the world’s wisdom, he says to them, “If anyone among you thinks he is wise”—not “if anyone is wise,” but “thinks he is wise among you”—“in this age let him become a fool.” He did not say simply “a fool,” but “in this age,” as people call us fools relative to this age. For such a person is truly a fool, and those doctrines are folly. And when you examine all Greek and barbarian philosophy simply, you will say that wherever it disagrees with Christ’s teaching it is folly. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness.”

I say it is no great thing if God, as God, catches the wise in their craftiness—but rather in Paul, who says, “For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but powerful with God for the tearing down of strongholds, tearing down reasonings and every height raised against the knowledge of God.” To understand this more clearly, picture Paul arriving in Athens and seeking opportunity among those he meets, so that some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers even clash with him; then by Christ’s grace he was catching hold of them and exposing their sophisms. Here I take “the wise” to mean the sophists—whoever spins entangled sophisms and does not teach truth.

And again: “The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.” It is no wonder if the Lord, by himself, knows that the reasonings of the wise are futile. But I want the Lord, come to be in me, to know that the reasonings of the wise are futile. For if Christ comes to be in me, he can set beside me how the reasonings of this world’s wise are futile, and how God’s wisdom alone shines, conquering and trampling every seeming wisdom.

1 Cor. 3:21–23: “So let no one boast in human beings. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.” Origen says: The one who can renounce all human beings and become wholly worthy of the boast that is in Christ does not boast in a human being. How, then, is death mine? So that I may die to sin; so that I may say, “If we died with him, we will also live with him.” For the other death—by which the sinning soul itself will die—is not mine. Present things too are ours: that we gather in the present age, hear the holy Scriptures, pray. And the future: when the perfect comes, then what is in part will be done away. And it is not possible to come to the future unless the present first becomes mine.

“All things are yours.” Among the Greeks a saying of this sort is admired: “All things belong to the wise, and nothing to the worthless.” But the word of God first taught that all things belong to the holy. Of the faithful, then, he says, the whole world of goods; of the unfaithful, not even an obol. For the unfaithful holds what he holds as a robber: not knowing how to use these things, nor knowing the God who made them, nor hearing the one who says, “Mine is the silver and mine the gold,” he does not hold them as his own. But we see that all things are ours; and of the faithful the whole world of goods, of the unfaithful not even an obol.

1 Cor. 4:1–5: “This is how one should regard us: as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required in stewards that one be found faithful. But with me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by a human day. I do not even examine myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby justified. It is the Lord who examines me. So do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will disclose the purposes of the hearts. Then each one will receive his praise from God.”

Origen says: The one who has not crossed over in the word to the grasp of the mysteries hidden in Scripture can be a servant of Christ, but cannot be a steward of God’s mysteries. For the steward has what is administered and knows the mysteries of God. Perhaps, then, the servant of Christ is understood according to the more common ministry, while the steward of God’s mysteries is understood according to the management that concerns the mysteries once known—so that he does not toss them about at random, nor hand them over unexamined, but first cleanses, prepares, and draws away from the world the one who is about to hear supra-worldly lessons, and only then speaks them.

english: of God. He administers the mysteries of God, for example, toward Luke so that he may be able to write the Gospel, and toward Timothy so that he may begin to be able to manage those in Ephesus who have received more—and to steward the mysteries of God. I even dare to say that in Corinth he became a servant of Christ, but in Ephesus a steward of God’s mysteries.

Having learned from the Savior’s words—“Who then is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord will set over his household to give the food allowance in season to his fellow servants?”—Paul says, “Moreover, it is required in stewards that one be found faithful.” For it is not enough to have come to know, nor should the one who knows speak at random; rather, understanding that one must give the food allowance in season to his fellow servants, he must see which of the fellow servants ought to receive a larger measure of God’s mysteries, or a smaller, and when. For if he administers the stewardship well and blamelessly, what promise does he have? “Over all his goods,” he says, “the master of the house will set him.” And if Paul fears and says these things about himself and about Cephas and Apollos, how much more must the stewards among us fear that they may be found faithful stewards.

Then about himself he says, “But with me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by a human day.” Those in Corinth examined as far as they could—not truly examining. For examining would be saying that Paul is better than Cephas and Apollos, and another’s examining would be saying that Peter far surpasses Paul; for in the Gospel Paul is not called an apostle. So Paul says that with him it is a very small thing to be examined by you. He was conscious in himself of the finest things, and that he did not fall under the Corinthians as people able to examine him; for “the spiritual person examines all things, yet he himself is examined by no one”—as elsewhere he says, “I have become a fool; you compelled me.” Something of that kind he means here too.

There is a human day, and there is a divine day, about which countless things are written, including “Behold, the day of the Lord comes.” So my examination, he says, cannot take place in a human day; for a human day cannot contain my examination. If I am going to be examined, I will be examined in the day of the Lord.

Then, more paradoxically conscious of himself, he says, “But I do not even examine myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself.” Here the Apostle’s conscience appears greatly purified—so much so that he dared to write not only to those then living, but so that generations until the end may also read what is said. True, then, is Paul when he says, “Become imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.” How Paul imitated Christ, hear: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me”; and Paul says, “I am not aware of anything against myself.” And he did not say, “I am not aware of any worthless deed against myself.” For if he had said that, we could say he is cleansed in works but not yet in words; or again, cleansed in these, while his heart still sinned. Now he seems to know in himself an excess of purity—not earlier when he persecuted, or when he came to the faith, but now when he was saying these things.

Then, lest he seem to have spoken above a human being, he adds and says, “But I am not thereby justified. For I,” he says, “am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby justified.” For it is possible that I know nothing against myself, and yet some sin of mine escapes me. For many such things happen in human nature that one sins not according to reason, not with grasping or assent, not with seeing that we have sinned. So that one who in all things is aware of nothing against himself says, “But I am not thereby justified; it is the Lord who examines me.”

As one who has passed beyond the examination of angels and of the other powers, he says this: “Until the Lord comes.” Since judgment lies ahead—and that of the Lord alone is true, who knows how to weigh thoughts and set words in a balance and search out all deeds and render to each of us what is due—therefore even if we condemn someone, let us not pass final sentence. For we do not know by what measure he sinned, nor with what disposition he sinned, nor whether he has good counterweights to his sin. If we become careful, we will not judge anything before the time, but will refer everything to the judgment of God through our Savior Jesus Christ.
Here it is said, “Do not judge anything before the time,” and what follows; but in another place in the letter: “Do you not judge those who are inside? But those outside God judges.”

english: So do the Scriptures have contradictions, and must we both judge and not judge under the same sense of judgment? If those entrusted to judge those inside do not judge those inside, the church is about to become, instead of God’s church, a synagogue of evildoers. Then, with those inside being judged, how is “Do not judge, that you may not be judged” true?

We say, then: those entrusted to judge those inside are not so senseless that, when judging those inside, they claim, “We are judging God’s judgment.” Rather, they make the judgment with a view to the stewardship of what benefits the church. If it benefits that this person be put out of the assembly, having judged that, they do it. And again they will take their stand toward what benefits—not judging God’s judgment, but the judgment given them. For the judgment that God judges in Christ it is impossible for us to judge; we neither search hearts nor know with what reasonings each person’s deeds were done. The hidden things the judges according to the Gospel leave to the Lord God; the manifest things, as it is said, “to you and to your children.” Whatever has reached them and is known among them, these they judge.

So never anticipating God’s judgment let us say, “So-and-so is lost,” or, blessing, “So-and-so is saved.” For we do not know how to measure and compare deeds with deeds, or reasonings, or thoughts. So do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will disclose the purposes of the hearts.

Of two things named, there ought to be a difference between them: some he called hidden things of darkness, others purposes of hearts. See, then, whether our sins are hidden things of darkness, and our brave deeds purposes of the hearts. For whatever we do well we do with counsel; but whatever we sin, we sin being in darkness. Since, then, some have these or those, and a human being does not know them, let us not judge anything before the time until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the purposes of the hearts. For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through the body, whether good or worthless.

I found a Gospel saying near this to expound: “Nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, and nothing covered that will not be revealed.” You see the Savior giving a difference between hidden things made manifest and covered things revealed. What, then, are the hidden and made-manifest if not the good? And what the covered and revealed if not the bad?

Someone who investigates everything might ask: why did he not say, “And then praise or blame will come to each from God,” but only “the praise”? One will explain it this way: he attached the more favorable word to God, keeping silent about the rest as not fitting him. But I will dare to say that God praises and accepts the good, while our evils the father of evils—the devil—does; and praise from God comes to the saints, while blame for those who have done blameworthy things comes from the devil. Therefore it is said to you by the Apostle, so that the one from the opposite side may be put to shame, having nothing worthless to say about us.

1 Cor. 4:6–8: “These things, brothers, I have applied to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn the saying, ‘Not beyond what is written,’ that none of you may be puffed up for the one against the other. For who distinguishes you? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? Already you are filled! Already you have become rich! Without us you have begun to reign! And would that you did reign, so that we might reign with you!”

Origen says: These things are written in a transfer shaped to the circumstances then—not so that we may know them only about Paul and Apollos, but so that in every generation, seeing what happens analogously to these things, we may take care lest we too fall into such things and, as in theaters that split over performances, we split over teachers.

But let us see the line, “So that in us you may learn, ‘Not beyond what is written.’” If someone with a lesser habit, before fulfilling what is written, wants to ascend to what is beyond what is written, he will not even understand what is written. For just as it is not possible to climb a ladder except by going the way from the lower steps according to one’s ability, so also with the divine lessons. english: They promise traditions and say, “These are beyond what is written; for our Savior handed these to the apostles in secret, and the apostles to so-and-so or so-and-so.” And thus through this myth-making they deceive the hearts of the simple. But the rest say, “It is written, ‘Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam in your own?’ and ‘Do not judge, that you may not be judged.’” For if we are one and bound to one another, we must not rise against one another. For “the one who humbles himself will be exalted,” and “the one who wants to be first among you must be last of all,” and “each should remain in that in which he was called.”

These and such things are written, so that none may be puffed up for the one against the other. For those who divided themselves—some wanting to be called of this one, some of that—fought one another, each eager to set their own teachers above the others, and then against the teachers themselves. “For who distinguishes you? Who appointed you of a party? Why are you not called teacher of all alike? What do you have that you did not receive? On what do you think highly? On fluency of speech? But God has granted you this. On knowledge? This too is a divine gift. On wonder-works? This also is the Spirit’s working. And if you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” No one thinks highly over another’s deposits; he watches over them to keep them for the one who gave them.

One must gather from the Scriptures what “distinguish” means, so that we may apply it to what is now said. “God stands in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes gods.” Here distinguishing appears as God’s work. Judging being something else—what falls on those worthy of judgment—it is good to be found a god in the assembly of gods, so that one is no longer judged but distinguished, and as it were entrusted one rank of those entrusted to the gods in assembly. But also in “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others distinguish,” distinguishing there seems taken as articulating—clarify what is said, distinguish it, and understand it. And in “The one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith,” the one distinguishing appears spoken of for blame. And again: “Welcome one another, not distinguishing with reasonings when you sin.” So from Scripture the word is sometimes set on the better and sometimes on the opposite.

Here, then, “distinguish” means: no one among those in Corinth distinguishes you or judges you; but you distinguish a steward of God’s mysteries and say, “I am of Paul,” and claim, “I of Cephas,” or say, “I am of Apollos.” Distinguishing the apostles is God’s work, not yours. Just as you must not judge, you must not distinguish the servants of the gospel. For in the distinction by which you distinguish the apostles, you distinguish and separate yourself, sinning. For Christ came to unite what had been distinguished, so that we would no longer be divided. If we are perfected so that the flesh no longer desires against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh—by putting to death the members that are on the earth—we will no longer be in distinction but as it were in mixture and in our gathering to the same. Let it also be understood more simply of various schisms.

Let us also see “What do you have that you did not receive?” For the wording is ambiguous. It can mean that every possession we have we have received from God; and again, “Why pretend to have what you did not receive?”—as when someone, not having received a gift from above from God, pretends to be in a gift, it is said to such a one who did not receive, “What do you have that you did not receive?” And if you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? english: teacher, but if he finds a second he also uses him, for he is unsated of good things; if he has a third as well, he also comes to the third. Not cutting off one for himself, he says, “I am of Paul,” or “of Cephas,” or “of Apollos.” Since, then, “being filled” suggests that when there are more teachers—Paul teaching, and Cephas, and Apollos—one who leans to one is not helped by all, therefore he says to the Corinthians, “Already you are filled?” Following this is “Already you have become rich?”—as in, “Have you gathered the wealth from Paul’s lessons and no longer need those from Apollos or from Cephas?” Or do you despise all, as stuffed and rich in every word and all knowledge? And following also: “Without us you have begun to reign?” For as far as you could you cut me off from the kingdom—and yourselves too—leaning to one from among the rest. And he does not say “without me” but “without us,” so as to include and make it common; “and would that you did reign, so that we might also reign with you.”

At once, perhaps, he also suggests a mystery at this place. For the lesser come more quickly into the promise, while the more perfect receive the promises later. And I will show this from Scripture: those allotted under Moses first received the promise; those allotted under Joshua later. And of all the righteous it is said, “These all, having been attested through faith, did not receive the promise, God having foreseen something better concerning us, so that they would not be perfected apart from us.” Therefore he says, “Without us you have begun to reign? And would that you did reign, so that we might also reign with you.” For when you the disciples and hearers reign, then it is necessary that we also arrive at the perfect kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus.

1 Cor. 4:9–10: “For I think God has exhibited us apostles last, as sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world and to angels and to human beings. We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored.” Origen says: The more one claims the true and heavenly first places, so much the more, from humility, he becomes last of all human beings. I think the Apostle meant something like this when he said, “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given.” Not that in holiness he was less than all the saints—for he neither thought this, nor if he said it would he speak truly—but among all believers he made himself lower, becoming gentle in the midst of all, as a nurse cherishes her own children.

Since, then, the apostles practiced being last by their own choice—and for every good practice, unless God witnesses and fills the practitioner’s will, the good end does not follow through the practitioner—therefore perhaps the Apostle said, “For I think God has exhibited us apostles last, as sentenced to death.” For even if I, he says, and the apostles have acted so that we become last, we still needed exhibition and grace from God to be perfected in being last to the world. And “I think” is as elsewhere he said, “I think I too have the Spirit of God.”

Fitting also for those exhibited last by God is becoming first with God; for it is true that the last become first. Fitting also for them is being sentenced to death. For the more perfectly one lives as a Christian, so much more is he death-bound. When does he not risk danger—reproving the sinner who is often stronger in life and able to punish, visiting places where Christ was not named, and laying a foundation strange and disturbing to hearers? Truly Paul said, “I die daily—by your boast which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

But as I search the word, “sentenced to death” can be taken two ways: one the way already said, by which one must always carry about the dying of Jesus in the body; another, the righteous is death-bound, being conformed to the death of Christ, always dying to the world. So it is fitting that God exhibit the apostles of Christ as both last and sentenced to death.

Then one must see “because we have become a spectacle to the world and to angels and to human beings.” If Paul contends and Peter, the angels of God hurry to this new spectacle to see a human being clothed in flesh wrestling against the principalities,

english: against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this world, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. And human beings also came to see a new spectacle—a herald and teacher of a new word. Thus Paul was a spectacle of all on earth and of the angels who rejoice over one sinner repenting.

Then such a one, as last in the world, rebukes the puffed up and says to them, “We are fools for Christ.” For Paul, giving me a command and saying, “If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may become wise,” much more himself kept becoming a fool in this world. For how was he not a fool in this world—announcing the crucified one and the resurrection of the dead and the things about the coming age, and persuading people to despise the present life? Then with irony: “You are wise in Christ.” For they were not truly wise in Christ; but saying this ironically he urged them to become wise in Christ. “You are honored, but we are dishonored”—he no longer added “you are honored in Christ.” For if you see many who seem to believe holding worldly ranks, say to them, if you yourself are humble in the world, “You are honored, but we are dishonored; we are weak, but you are strong.” For nothing is weaker than a true Christian as toward this world.

1 Cor. 4:15: “For though you have countless guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.” Origen says: These things seem simplest and to need no exposition; yet they have hidden meanings. No man is put under a guardian unless he is a child and incomplete. And he would not write these things to the Ephesians but to the Corinthians, to whom he says, “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able. But neither are you able even now, for you are still fleshly.” And: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual people but as to fleshly, as to infants in Christ.” Still this too must be noted: if we need a guardian, the one entrusted must give the pattern—the word, the life—to our good order. So a father is the one who first sowed Christianity in a soul; a guardian is the one after him who receives the child and leads him.

4:16: “I urge you, then, brothers, become imitators of me.” That is: as I practice moderation, practice it; as I suffer, suffer; boast from sufferings, not from gifts. 4:17: “For this reason I sent you Timothy, who is my beloved child and faithful in Christ, who will remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach everywhere in every church.” He showed both his disposition toward them by sending Timothy, and his affection for Timothy by naming him beloved child; and his other virtue by calling him faithful in the Lord. This one, he says, will recount my deeds; for he calls deeds “ways.” These he did not say “he will teach,” but that “he will remind.” The word charges them with forgetfulness; for they had been eyewitnesses of apostolic virtue. He added that he is accustomed to bring this teaching to all the churches.

Having charged all in common, against the one who fornicated he then issues the vote. 4:18: “Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you.” Foreseeing his repentance, the divine Paul does not set the name, lest he become known to all human beings, but indefinitely said “some.”

4:19–20: “And I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power.” Origen says: By “talk” he means fluency of speech, as elsewhere, “even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge”; by “power,” that from God. For when the word is from God it has power; therefore it is written, “The Lord will give a word to those who evangelize with much power.” And trusting more in power, the apostles visited the churches and cities than in talk. For it is not that if someone phrases well he thereby has the kingdom of God; but where there is power in words, there is the kingdom of God—which also drives out the sin reigning in souls and prepares God’s kingdom to come within us.

4:21–5:2: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness? english: so that the one who did this deed might be removed from among you.” Origen says: Neither God nor his divine disciples always use kind words toward hearers, nor always harsh ones, but sometimes these and sometimes those. Since, then, Paul’s word had a rod and also a spirit of gentleness and kindness, he asks the Corinthians, not wanting to use the harsher too rashly and quickly—not that the rod comes without love, but that love is hidden in the one holding the rod and does not show the love in the severity of the rebuke. Then he adds the cause of such a question, saying, “It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you of a kind not even among the nations.”

We learn that we must be charmed concerning sexual immorality lest we fall; and another lesson, so that those not aware of sexual immorality in themselves, yet aware of those gathering who fornicate, may not be puffed up—knowing that they too are sinners because the one gathering with them is a sinner. For he charges the whole church about one who fornicated, and charges their puffing up as not according to reason, especially because a fornicator is still among them. And third we learn that there are differences of sexual immoralities, so that there is a heaviest and another lesser and another still lesser. Therefore in God’s judgment fornicators are not simply judged, nor will they receive the same condemnation for having fornicated; but quantity and quality increase the punishment, and choice and time.

In Corinth, then, someone contracted an unlawful marriage; he took his stepmother. But the Apostle calls such a marriage sexual immorality, and of a kind one does not even hear among the nations—to teach us that if ever we marry unlawfully, the supposed marriage is not counted to us as marriage but as sexual immorality. Then leaving him he brings the charge against his company: “And you are puffed up and have not rather mourned, so that the one who did this deed might be taken from among you.” He rebukes all as having received him badly. For when the one who sinned is in the midst and we who seem to ourselves aware of better things are puffed up, it is said, “And you are puffed up.”

1 Cor. 5:3–5: “For I, though absent in body yet present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, the one who has done this thing. When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus, you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.” Origen says: Not for destruction of the soul, not for destruction of the spirit, but for destruction of the flesh—for so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord he is handed over. For Paul cast such a one out, not knowing that he would repent and turn, but wanting to discipline him. For it is one thing to cut someone off as incapable of repentance and turning, another to put him off for the present and cast him from the flock, as a shepherd casts out a sheep with mange so that the pasture of that wound not spread over the whole flock.

So let those living badly be healed outside the flock, confessing and mourning their own sins, bringing the things of repentance in fasts and mourning and weeping and the like. For they are handed over to be disciplined so that their flesh may be destroyed—that is, the mindset of the flesh—not so that he may touch their soul, not so that he may drive them out of their minds, not so that he may do anything else, but so that he may receive authority only over their flesh, not I giving the authority but the power of Jesus in me.

From the better part he named the whole salvation, lest he say “and spirit and soul and body be saved in the day of the Lord,” but “the spirit be saved,” naming from the better the salvation of the whole human being. For as one to be saved he orders him received into the church in the second letter. To be absent in body and present in spirit belongs to Paul and those like him; for he said elsewhere, “For though I am absent in flesh, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.” But none of us can say, “I am present and see the church’s excellences or the order and the firmness of faith in Christ.”

english: Such was Elisha. Even when he was not present in the body, he went along with Gehazi in the spirit and said to him: “Was not my heart with you when he took the two talents of silver and the garments from Naaman the Syrian?” (2 Kings 5:26). Did Elisha then have this gift, while Paul, the apostle of Christ who was zealous for the greater gifts—and above all that he might prophesy—did not have such a gift? I declare, and I speak with confidence, that Paul was not only an apostle but also a prophet. He was such when he said: “People will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents” (2 Timothy 3:2); for he said these things not as an apostle but as a prophet. And he says: “The Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith” (1 Timothy 4:1). Which Spirit? As if he were saying: the Spirit in me. Having this gift, then, even if he was absent in the body, wherever he wished he was present in the spirit; for he was not alone present in the spirit, but the power of Jesus was also present.

Clean out the old leaven, then, that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:7–8).

The one who has put off the old man with his deeds and has nothing of the old leaven in himself, but has made a new lump according to Christ Jesus, has kept the feast of unleavened bread. Then after the feast of unleavened bread the new leaven appears. Jesus the Christ is the new leaven. Let us therefore first eat unleavened bread, abstaining from every malice and wickedness. Teaching about these things the apostle says: “Clean out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened.” Something of this sort happens among the Jews: when the day of unleavened bread dawns, they clean out all old leaven, searching every place of the house lest leaven be found there. In the same way you also examine the storehouses within yourself lest leaven be there somewhere, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. Since in Corinth some were holy and others were not such but sinners—as we said earlier in the preface of the letter—on account of the praiseworthy ones he says “as you are unleavened.” For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Seeing that according to the law of Moses the Passover comes first and the lamb is slain, and then after the lamb they eat unleavened bread, for this reason he said: Already the Passover has been sacrificed—Christ. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth—sincerity according to the way of life, truth according to knowledge; for in both the true unleavened bread is characterized.

I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with the sexually immoral—not at all meaning the immoral of this world, or the greedy and robbers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world. But now I write to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is sexually immoral or greedy or an idolater or a reviler or a drunkard or a robber—not even to eat with such a one (1 Corinthians 5:9–11).

Some have supposed from this saying that before the former letter to the Corinthians another letter had been written by the apostle which is not now preserved; and that he wrote to them not to associate with the sexually immoral, so far as the present wording goes. But having heard that the Corinthians were disturbed, thinking he meant they must not associate even with the immoral of the world—which is impossible, for one who lives in the world cannot avoid dealing with Gentile coworkers, traders, and others of that sort—he clarifies, they say, what had then been left out: I do not mean the immoral of this world, but those who are named brothers yet are not honorable. english: this letter itself: that in this letter I wrote that you should not associate with the sexually immoral—and by “immoral” I mean these, not those. The apostle seems by comparison of fornicators to say that those among us who are immoral are far worse. For the outsider who fornicates does not destroy a temple of God, does not make the members of Christ members of a prostitute, and does not leaven the whole lump. And that one, whenever he wishes, repents and has forgiveness of sins; but the one who fornicates after the faith, even if he later repents, does not have forgiveness of sins in the same way, though he can cover the sin. For he says: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven”—of those who came over from the nations—“and whose sins are covered”—of those who sin after the faith yet cover them with good works, for example covering license with abundant self-control (Psalm 32:1).

And not at all with the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy, or robbers, or idolaters. Just as there are fornicators of the world and fornicators called to Christ, so also there are greedy people of this world and of the church. Let us therefore guard against greed even in the smallest matters; for it too is yoked to the sin of fornication. And third he names certain robbers, when they seize what belongs to their neighbors. And there are also some idolaters among us besides the idolaters of this world—those who want to teach that idolatry is a matter of indifference. This sin is found especially among those in military service. They say: Necessity is laid on me; the army requires this; I risk my head if I do not sacrifice or, dressed in white, offer frankincense according to the customs of the world’s army—and such a one still calls himself a Christian. With such a one, he says, do not even eat. And the denier of God in a time of persecution is also an idolater among us. So he says: I wrote to such a one who is not yet out of the world not to associate, since otherwise you would need to go out of the world. But now I have written to you not to associate if anyone is named a brother. Well does he no longer call such a one a brother, but a brother only as far as the name.

These evils many of us can know in ourselves that we do not have. But at what follows I fear for myself as well, lest somehow I be liable to the other sins. For he says: or a reviler or a drunkard or a robber—with such a one do not even eat. With how great evils he numbered the reviler together with the fornicator, the greedy, and the idolater! Therefore the reviler too is already an enemy of the church. For this reason we hear the Lord saying: “Bless those who curse you” (Luke 6:28), and the apostle saying: “When reviled, we bless” (1 Corinthians 4:12); for a reviler will not inherit the kingdom of God. We must therefore keep the mouth clean. For what is it to me to judge those outside? Let drunkards be outside; I eat and spend time with fornicators—does their little leaven not harm me? Does it not leaven this whole lump?

For what is it to me to judge those outside? Is it not those inside you judge? And those outside God will judge (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). He has permitted all of us to judge those inside who sin. We ourselves bring the sin up to the bishop, that such a one may be cast out of the church by law. And you will remove the wicked person from among yourselves. From these too remove the wicked one; but seek lest, while wishing to remove the wicked from outside, you have the wicked one within yourself. Therefore do everything to remove the wicked from yourself; for when that one has gone out, Christ Jesus will dwell in you.

Does any of you, having a matter against another, dare to go to law before the unjust and not before the saints? Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is judged by you, are you unworthy of the smallest courts? Do you not know that we will judge angels—how much more matters of this life? (1 Corinthians 6:1–3).

He puts to shame those in Corinth who sin and are busy with law courts and worldly needs and miseries, and says: You were called to this, that when perfected you may judge angels; will you not rather be able, if ever a brother goes to law with a brother, to judge the brothers’ worldly affairs? So if you have worldly courts, and so on. Truly sometimes the cases of those judged are such that they do not need a wise judge, but rather you should seat those who are despised in the church; yet sometimes the cases of those on trial may be such as to need a wise judge as well.
