english: church; and there will be blame on those judged when they need even the despised rather than the wise. For the one who follows the Word, if he needs a judge, needs rather a wise one, that he may be admonished by the wisdom of the wise man who brings him words that build up. Therefore seat those who are despised in the church. I say this to your shame. Is it so, that there is not among you anyone wise who will be able to decide between his brother? He charges the Corinthian church that, though seated in the middle of Greece, they had no true wise men, although he had said earlier that many among them profess wisdom—on whose account he also said: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (1 Corinthians 3:19). But some are wise of this age, and others wise according to God. Paul knew those former ones; therefore he says: Is it so, that there is not among you a wise man who will be able to decide between his brother?

But brother goes to law with brother, and this before unbelievers? We have rulers of the church to whom we ought to bring our judgments, that we may not be laughed at in the courts of the nations. Already it is altogether a defeat for you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded? (1 Corinthians 6:7). Let us withdraw from the judgments of Gentile tribunals, from having lawsuits and disputes. For the one who has lawsuits with his brother is already defeated, and the one who is wronged has conquered; the one beaten and reviled who does not repay the one doing these things has conquered, for he keeps the command that says: Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded? But you wrong and defraud, and that your brothers. Everyone who does these things sins; and the more honorable the person wronged, the heavier the sin. For if someone wrongs the blessed one, he wrongs Christ in effect and defrauds Christ.

Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? If the kingdom of God is in Christ, and Christ is righteousness, the righteous inherits the kingdom of God in Christ who is righteousness; and accordingly the one in the opposite state does not inherit the kingdom of God. Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral… Let no one deceive you with persuasive words: “God is merciful, kind, and loving toward humankind; he forgives sins.” We must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive the things done through the body, whether good or bad (2 Corinthians 5:10). Let no one make excuses: I was young; I was unmarried; before taking a wife I committed fornication. Why then did you not take a wife? Do you not believe that if anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him? Do you take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? The one who fornicates acts impiously toward the God of all.

Do not be deceived, then: neither the sexually immoral nor idolaters will inherit the kingdom of God; and so neither adulterers. The one who fornicates destroys the temple of God; the adulterer, in addition, also sins against the husband. Neither adulterers, then; nor the soft / effeminate. We exhort you also, children, to keep your own season pure and not to be defiled with such womanish pollution. Nor will men who lie with men inherit the kingdom of God; and may it be far from the church that even one such be found. Then he descends also to sins that seem lesser, saying: nor thieves. This sin of theft nearly all who serve in the army commit, not content with their wages, as the gospel taught, but shaking people down and bringing false charges. And those who lie in business are thieves, not inheriting the kingdom of God; and so also those who overreach in business are greedy; and others are drunkards; and he says revilers also do not inherit the kingdom of God. Therefore let sin reign over no one; for the kingdom of God must be pure from all sins and stumblings, that God may reign.

All things are lawful for me, but not all things are helpful. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be mastered by anything (1 Corinthians 6:12). One must stand above the things over which one has received authority—things which, even if we do them, we will not sin. For those who live more ambitiously live in this way. Do we not have authority to eat and drink? Do we not have authority to take along a sister as wife, as also the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? (1 Corinthians 9:4–5).

english: of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working? But we have not used this right. Therefore it was permitted to the apostle to do all these things in the places I set out; yet examining them with a view to his own advantage and to the ordering of the church he saw that it is permitted—if he does it, he will not sin—yet he does better by not using the right. And again: every virgin is permitted to marry; but the good and noble woman abstains from marriage not as if marriage were forbidden, but having raised the right higher and wishing to be pure in body and spirit she remains a virgin. And when a husband has died, remarriage is not wholly forbidden: “For if the husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). But when the good woman hears: “She is more blessed if she remains as she is, according to my judgment” (1 Corinthians 7:40), she does not use the right. “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be mastered by anyone.” The saying has something higher: for if our wrestling is not against blood and flesh but against the rulers, against the authorities (Ephesians 6:12), when the authority masters me I have been mastered by it; but if I conquer every authority, I will not be mastered by anyone.

Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food—and God will destroy both this and these. But the body is not for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And God raised the Lord and will also raise us through his power (1 Corinthians 6:13–14).

Do not think that just as the stomach came to be for foods and foods for the stomach, so also the body came to be for intercourse. If you wish to learn the primary reason why it came to be, listen: that it may be a temple for the Lord, and that the soul, being holy and blessed, may become, as it were by serving, a priest of the Holy Spirit within you. For Adam also had a body in paradise, yet in paradise itself Adam did not know Eve his wife, but when he was cast out after the disobedience. I say these things not as marking off marriage; for I know that if anyone is not continent he ought to marry; for it is better to marry than to burn (1 Corinthians 7:9). Yet even if the matter is conceded, it is not primarily but because of weakness. For what is primary is to live in chastity and purity and to have leisure for prayer. For of the one already raised with Christ and made conformed to his resurrection and to the newness of life, the body ought to belong to nothing except the Lord.

Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? (1 Corinthians 6:15). Human bodies are instruments of the soul; and when the soul rules, the body serves and is used for whatever the soul wishes. But the Word especially wills that our bodies no longer be energized by our own soul but by Christ himself; therefore Paul says: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). They become members of Christ, then, when we move everything according to his word.

Flee sexual immorality. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body (1 Corinthians 6:18). Someone will ask whether every sin is outside the body. For someone will say: Drunkenness is a sin; taking oneself out of life by hanging or by a cliff is a sin; is this sin also outside the body? In addition, then, however many sins we commit—even if we commit murders—yet if we remain uncorrupted and have not tasted the corruption that belongs to intercourse, we are not said to have been corrupted by having murdered. But since both incorruption and corruption concern the nature that is without taste of sexual pleasure—for we say “the virgin was corrupted,” and again “the young man is uncorrupted,” or “he was corrupted”—every sin that a person commits is outside the body (1 Corinthians 6:18). Since therefore a ransom was given for you, the blood of Christ, and he took you from the authority of the devil, glorify God in your body, that your body may become worthy of blessedness as of those who have loved incorruption, as also the apostle says: the grace of God be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption (Ephesians 6:24).

Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of the cases of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband give to the wife her due, and likewise also the wife to the husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does (1 Corinthians 7:1–4).

People who sin, speaking generally, sin in two ways: by falling short of the commandments or by going beyond them. For when we do not live from knowledge and, not knowing the measures of righteousness, we slip, and sometimes by overshooting the rule in the fancy of doing something better we fall away from what is set before us. The proper weight, then—which is neither large nor small but commensurate—is to know how one ought to live. You have been bound with a wife: you make one large weight; you do not care for the wife but say: I am able to practice continence and live more purely. But see that your wife is being destroyed, unable to bear your purity, for whom Christ died. Something of this sort happened in Corinth, and there was disorder in the households of the brothers, husbands in one place and wives in another trying to practice continence and rising up against one another. So those in Corinth wrote a letter to the apostle about this, and to that letter the apostle writes back what has been written above. He neither stretched the word about chastity so as to abolish the word about marriage, nor, preferring marriage, abolished the word about virginity, as a good steward; but throughout the whole discourse he somehow keeps his wish and exhorts to purity; and having conceded condescension, he again exhorts to practice chastity; and having exhorted to practice chastity, he again brings them to the need to condescend to the weakness of the weaker. He began not from the lesser things—for that would not have been fitting—but from the more perfect matters, saying: Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me, it is good for a man not to touch a woman—as if: I praise you for having wished to live chastely, those who withdrew from mixture with the wife; but reckon not only your own interest but also the wife’s. For love does not seek its own (1 Corinthians 13:5). Therefore because of the cases of sexual immorality let each have his own wife, and each her own husband. Not because of his own fornication should the stronger keep his own wife, but lest somehow the wife fornicate because of the husband’s continence, and the husband because of the wife’s. english: to heal human weakness and to arrange the matters in those places most becomingly; therefore he said a due is owed from the husband and to the husband from the wife. Then, lest he shame those in marriage as being slaves of one another who must not come to the exercise of purity without agreement, he says: The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. The husband therefore has authority over the wife’s body, and having authority, if he wishes, let him not use the authority; “but we did not use this right,” says the apostle, teaching this, I think, when he says: Do we not have a right to take along a sister as wife, as also the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? (1 Corinthians 9:5). Does the wife then have authority over the husband’s body and is she unable not to use the authority? The word “likewise” set twice gives us to understand that the husband must not think that in the matters of marriage he excels the wife; there is likeness and equality for those married toward one another.

Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer, and be together again (1 Corinthians 7:5). You both ought to know that prayer from a man’s and a woman’s purity is not the same as prayer from intercourse. For if Greeks sometimes practice chastity before idols, how much more you who pray to the God of all? It is good, then, to condescend because of weakness, and to hold back because of prayers. Moses also purifies the people and says for three days not to approach a woman, that by having purified beforehand they may become hearers of God (Exodus 19:15). And in the Kingdoms, when Abathar or Ahimelech the priest wishes to set holy bread before David fleeing Saul’s plot, what does he say except: If the young men are clean from a woman?—not from a strange woman but from a wife (1 Samuel 21:4–5). Then, that someone may receive the bread of the Presence, he ought to be clean from a woman; but that he may receive the greater breads than the Presence, over which the name of God and of Christ and of the Holy Spirit has been invoked, how much more ought someone to be cleaner, that he may truly receive the breads unto salvation and not unto judgment?

Many think “deprive” is said only of gold or silver or something of that sort; but the apostle clearly named deprivation also concerning those in marriages who practice chastity unseasonably and without agreement. Once for all, simply, the one who does not render what is owed deprives the one to whom he owes by not rendering the due. Sometimes a person is shut in so that he cannot render two dues at once; therefore it is written that he may render the necessary due. What I mean will be clear thus: it is not possible both to render prayers to God as one ought and for the married man to render the due to the wife; therefore if the debt toward God presses, one must deprive the other. Hear him saying: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer and be together again—as if prayer sent up is not pure even for those who have come together, even if they have come together lawfully. One must also abstain from a woman in the time of her period, and it is counted a great charge to come together with a woman who is in her period. In Ezekiel’s catalog of brave deeds and of sins it is written that he will not approach a woman in her separation (Ezekiel 18:6). And one must be wholly pure also from one’s own wife in a time of prayer and fasting.

And again, he says, be together, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. This I say by way of concession, not of command (1 Corinthians 7:5–6). Everywhere he loosens the word because of weakness, and again tightens it to turn the hearers. I wish all people to be as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that (1 Corinthians 7:7). Marriage breathes of gift when the measures are kept—those of agreement. And one can truly say of some that for this one marriage is a gift, when there is no disorder, when there is all peace, all agreement. Yet to say that marriage of a believer with a Gentile woman, or of a Gentile with a believing woman, is a gift from God—this I would not say. For the gift of God cannot reach the Gentiles; if she believes, if she is saved, then she will begin to receive the gift.

english: Those from Marcion also use this saying, and without sense they forbid marriage, saying that chastity is a command of the other god whom they invented beside the Creator. Yet from the saying itself one can prove to them that they forbid marriage badly, and badly divide the Godhead. For if there is a gift to one in this way and to another in that, marriage also is a gift; if marriage is a gift, marriage the gift is badly forbidden; if the one in this way and the other in that are from God, it is clear that one God is the giver of chastity and the giver of marriage, and one is the God of the law and of the gospel, whom the prophets first proclaimed and later Christ Jesus.

But I say to the unmarried and to the widows that it is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not practicing self-control, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. To the married I give charge—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband—but if she is separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband—and that a husband not send away a wife. To the rest I say, I not the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:8–12).

Some among us teach beyond what is written; and thinking they are doing something, when they ought to exhort to single marriage without laying a snare on those who cannot, they do not do this, but impose necessity and wish not to gather the twice-married nor to share with them as with those who have transgressed, not respecting even the apostle’s voices. For the one who says to the unmarried and the widows, if they are not continent let them marry, openly permitted after the first marriage, after a woman has been widowed, to marry—while blaming the one who marries and the one who is married; for he said: If they are not continent, let them marry. See whether not being continent is not already an accusation—as when it is said to Christian people: Better to marry than to burn—he naming as burning the desire of the flesh not quenched by the Word but mastering the sinner’s soul. We therefore, taught by the apostle, do not forbid remarriage; for by comparison with burning, remarriage is more choiceworthy. Yet when something is thought better by comparison with evils, that thing is clearly not good. The second marriage is not temperance; it is not according to the nature of Adam the first-formed; for one cannot say to the second wife: This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Genesis 2:23). Abraham had also Hagar, and came to be also with Keturah; yet when he died, none was laid with him except the wife by nature; for Abraham and Sarah were in the tomb. And Jacob too, even if he had been with Rachel and with Leah and also with the maidservants, yet in the tomb only Leah was with him. With the mystical economy of the fathers; yet surely even now the one who takes a second does not say: I am fulfilling a mystical economy. For Paul will come saying: Tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written: So-and-so had two sons, and so on; it will not also be said over him: These things are allegorized, for these women are two covenants; for these things happened typically to them, but were written for us upon whom the ends of the ages have come (Galatians 4:21–24; 1 Corinthians 10:11).

I say to the widows and to the unmarried that it is good for them if they remain as I also am. This is a second good; for there is another good first before this: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. What second good? It is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not continent, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. Therefore those in first marriages who have not yet experienced second ones should practice chastity, that if something human happens they may not, caught untrained, behave shamefully. Better, then, to marry a second marriage—for he does not mean the first here, as is clear from the wording “to burn.” From here he passes to another legislation: To the married I give charge, not I but the Lord; the legislation toward the married is not from me but from the Lord. english: of prayers and of holy childbearing and of all things in which Christians must share, he says that marriage is not alien to God. I charge, then—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband. The primary point is this: a yoking that has already been bound must not be loosed. But if she is also separated—for many causes of separation can arise; for example if fornication happens to the wife, it is a sin to keep the wife who has fornicated. If then she is also separated and some cause of separation arises, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband. Likewise I also want a husband to be such that he not send away a wife. To the rest I say, I not the Lord. To those who have married I do not legislate, but the Lord; to those not married but unequally yoked with unbelievers I do not have a law to give from God; for they are not even worthy of God’s laws; but let them hear us. And I will use what is written in the law to make the matters of the place understood. The laws according to Moses—some are God’s, and some are Moses’. And knowing this difference of God’s laws and Moses’ laws, the Lord said concerning those legislated by God: For God said, Honor father and mother; and concerning those by Moses: Moses, because of your hardness of heart, allowed you to dismiss your wives (Matthew 19:8). If you keep the matters of the book of divorce you will find the law written not from a command of the Lord. Moses then, serving God, gave second laws beside the laws of God; Paul, serving the gospel, gave second laws to those of the church after the laws from God through Jesus Christ. And it is good to hear laws from the Lord rather than to hear laws of Paul the apostle. For even if he is holy, still he has laws far lesser than the laws of the Lord.

For the unbelieving husband is made holy in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy in the brother (1 Corinthians 7:14). As a kind of blending happens of the two, husband and wife, into one flesh, as of wine and water; and as the believer imparts holiness to the Gentile spouse, or the reverse—the believing woman to the unbelieving husband—so also the unbeliever imparts pollution to the believing wife, or the unbelieving wife to the believing husband. Why then does he say the unbeliever is made holy by receiving something from the believer, and is not also profaned by receiving something from the unbelieving part? For each, conversing from the abundance of the heart with the other, either imparts or receives, and in time the one entirely conquers the other. And what need, he says, of such a contest and danger? For either he will succeed or fail, and either he will lose his soul as well or, after much toil, scarcely be able to gain. Therefore it is good, before a person is forestalled, carefully to look not only at this but also at what is coming, and having looked either not to marry or, marrying, to marry in the Lord. For a wife is bound as long as her husband lives; but if the husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39). We do not hear the “only in the Lord,” but we read “she is free to be married to whom she wishes,” and we no longer set beside it “only in the Lord.” And yet even there, when he said “only in the Lord,” he again checked the word saying she is more blessed if she remains so, according to my judgment. So the apostle, having said the more auspicious thing—“For she is made holy”—left us to understand the other.

Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping God’s commandments. Let each remain in the calling in which he was called (1 Corinthians 7:18–20). It will seem that he has unseasonably cast beside the word about marriage and chastity, since no inquiry had arisen about those from circumcision who believe not needing to draw the foreskin, and again those in uncircumcision not needing to be circumcised, and about “Were you called a slave? Do not be concerned,” and what follows. Perhaps then he took slavery and freedom as a paradigm of the married and the unmarried, calling circumcised the one who has put away the wife and uncircumcised the one who has married? english: this also here he names a slave the one called after marriage, and free the unmarried. What is said about circumcision and about slaves is therefore said with a view to the place. Yet it is not out of place sometimes to use the saying against those who think after the faith one must be circumcised from a reverence—yet a reverence not according to knowledge—because of what is written in the old covenant about circumcision. Again it is not good, because of certain ones from circumcision who believe and think circumcision brings them shame and wish to draw a foreskin, to use the saying that says: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. And there is reason to say to such that in itself circumcision is a matter of indifference. So now it is neither about circumcision nor about uncircumcision, but about the unmarried and the married: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised—as if he were saying: Let him not draw a wife; he has already been circumcised; he put away a wife; let him not marry another. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised—as if: You were called in marriage; do not put away your wife. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing. Since some think the unmarried has something more in this respect than the married, and the married something less than the unmarried by the very fact of having married, we wish, he says, to teach that in its own account celibacy is indifferent and in its own account marriage is indifferent. For the one who is unmarried and truly pure from every mixture, yet living badly in other ways, may gain no benefit from celibacy; and someone in marriage, doing the things of marriage in order and season, keeping the rest of the way of life, may be no less than the unmarried. That celibacy itself and purity itself are indifferent we will prove thus. If only those from the church practiced celibacy, one might say that celibacy in its own account is something pure and divine; but now one can find also those unmarried with a base intention. Those from Marcion also practice celibacy and purity, but not as the church’s people do; for these do so to please the God who created the world, those so as not to cooperate with the god of the world. Celibacy is adorned by an ecclesiastical life and word, by pure knowledge and truth. So also the unmarried is indifferent in his own account; and it is possible also for one in marriage to be without blame, as we have already given. Circumcision then is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, both according to the wording and according to what is set before us. But what is it that saves? Keeping God’s commandments. For everyone who looses one of these least commandments and teaches people so—he did not say will not enter the kingdom of the heavens but will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens (Matthew 5:19). And if the one who loosed one of the least commandments will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens, where will the one who loosed two commandments be found? Let each therefore remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called in marriage? Do not envy the unmarried. Were you called unmarried? Do not by all means draw a foreskin, if you are able to live more purely.

Were you called a slave? Do not be concerned about it; but if you are also able to become free, rather use it. For the one called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise the one called free is Christ’s slave. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Brothers, let each remain with God in that in which he was called (1 Corinthians 7:21–24). He named a slave of necessity the married man; for the husband is a slave of the wife, not having authority over his own body, and the wife of the husband; for she does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. english: called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; as if: Were you called a slave? Know this, that you are not only not a slave, but you also have something of freedom because of the Lord. For the freedman is neither purely free nor still a slave, so that the one wholly pure is free and the one in marriage a slave; but when he is a slave in the Lord, then we say he is the Lord's freedman. And the one called free is a slave not of a wife but of the Word of God. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. With all your strength understand the one who bought us out, the Word of God; let us propitiate the blood poured out for us. We were saying in the word about unmarried and married that he tightens and loosens the word. So also here he has done, saying: Do not become slaves of human beings; for he as it were tightens and makes the word sharper, exhorting those able, as far as possible, to live purely, and each to live purely in the calling in which he was called. And one must know that the other interpreters have given the sense about uncircumcision and circumcision according to the letter; for customarily, they say, he passes from what is before him to other things, legislating for all what is fitting.

Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy (1 Corinthians 7:25). Of the commandments some are commanded, and some are not commanded but left free and entrusted to choice by God. For those without which one cannot be saved—these are the ones commanded; but the greater ones than the commanded, which even if we do not do we are saved, are not a command of God. Hear, he says, the gospel of Jesus Christ teaching in it and saying: when you have done all that is commanded you, you ought to say we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do (Luke 17:10). And if, when I do all that is commanded, I am an unprofitable servant, when will I flee being an unprofitable servant? If being more ambitious you ascend from what is commanded; for example: if I keep "you shall not commit adultery" and not looking at a woman to desire her, I have done what I ought. But if I remain a virgin, not ordered and not commanded, I no longer say over the achievement of virginity: we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought. So also on the remaining commandments: if I do not steal or overreach, we ought to say we are unprofitable servants. But if I sell all that I have and give to the poor, I no longer say I am unprofitable; I have done what I ought. Therefore the apostle says: Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy. For in the Lord's saying to the disciples not all receive the word but those to whom it has been given, and he adds: let the one who is able to receive it receive it (Matthew 19:11–12); he did not command, but left it free. So I give an opinion, says the apostle, and to show that the Lord speaks in him he said as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy.

I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity, that it is good for a person to be thus (1 Corinthians 7:26). By necessity he means the sojourn in the body, as also elsewhere he says: but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake (Philippians 1:24). Four times in the place the apostle named the good; for he says first: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; second: it is good for them if they remain as I also am; third: I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity; fourth: it is good for a person to be thus. You see how many things said about chastity are named with the good; but whatever is said about marriage, with the marrying person's not sinning.

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be loosed. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife (1 Corinthians 7:27). Through the whole discourse, as has been said, he tightens and loosens, that the hearer, taking it in his own authority, may judge what he is able and to what exercise he can give himself. So also here he turned away from loosing marriage, and again exhorts to live purely. Therefore he called the married husband bound; and if to be bound is a circumstance, one must flee circumstances as far as possible. english: if the virgin also marries, she has not sinned; again he did not say "good," but "she has not sinned." But such will have affliction in the flesh (1 Corinthians 7:28). For how will they not have affliction when what was said to the woman comes upon the married woman: In pain you will bear children, and your turning will be toward your husband, and he will rule over you (Genesis 3:16)? From all these the virgin is free, set free by purity, awaiting a bridegroom of blessing. Every marriage happens in darkness; therefore not in beds and wantonness (Romans 13:13). But Christ's marriage, when he receives his church, happens in the light. Why then do virgins enter the wedding with lamps and oil that lasts? Because that marriage is of seemliness. The one joined to flesh is one body; but the one joined to spirit is one spirit (1 Corinthians 6:16–17). And what is more seemly than a soul joined to spirit and united with it, no longer being a soul but becoming what the spirit is? For of marriage it was said: the two will become one flesh; but of the one joined to the Lord: he will be one spirit.

Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who shepherds a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock? Do I say these things according to a human way? Or does not the law also say these things? For in the law of Moses it is written: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing (1 Corinthians 9:7–9). As a God-fearing soldier the apostle says: Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? As one entrusted with God's field and farming the church: Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? As a disciple of the good shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep: Who shepherds a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock? And as a soldier he also teaches us to serve, saying: No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please the one who enlisted him (2 Timothy 2:4); as a farmer he also teaches us to farm: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). And about shepherds the prophets taught us, recounting the wages of the good and announcing the punishments of those who shepherd otherwise. And the apostle will seem to one not attending to the Scripture to have forgotten what is before him through these things; but the truth is not so—he holds to the word. It is before him to teach about food offered to idols, that even if someone professing knowledge says he is not harmed by using idol-food, yet if he becomes a cause of harm to others, he ought to have cared for his neighbor, lest on his pretext others be destroyed. For this he takes the examples and says: Not in every case, if we have authority over something, ought we to make full use of the authority. For whether he is a soldier, he does not serve so as to secure nothing for himself from the rations; or a farmer, he is not content with the wage but eats from the grape; or a shepherd, besides the wage he shares the milk. So also I ought, besides the promises laid up for me from having served or farmed or shepherded well, to share in this world the things needed from those under me as soldiers, those farmed, those shepherded. Yet even if I have authority over the things needed, looking to the building up of people I do not make full use of the authority, in awe of giving some cutting-off to the gospel of Christ, or of giving a pretext to those who walk disorderly and work nothing but are busybodies (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Just as I do not use the authority I received from the Word, in the same way you also who claim to be wise ought not to use the authority but to provide for the building up of neighbors. And if the word seems to some to be without witness and spoken by human reasoning, let him hear the law saying: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing, and what follows.

Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or does he speak entirely for our sake? For it was written for our sake, that the one plowing ought to plow in hope and the one threshing to share in hope. If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your fleshly things? (1 Corinthians 9:9–11). Therefore these things were said for our sake who have received the new covenant, and they were written about human beings, the saying being understood spiritually according to the divine apostle. And after sowing the newly broken ground he says: I watch the seeds, lest the birds of the heaven come and take the seed; and when it bears fruit and makes fruits of righteousness and when it is already white toward harvest, it is then permitted me to take. For he will not be scandalized when he remembers how much I have toiled that I may plow his soul, that I may sow, how I persisted up to the point his seed came finished to the threshing floor. And for this reason it is permitted me to take foods from him. But I have not by all means used the authority; yet I do this in hope, to present the produce to the master of the house; for I am a farmer; not that I may take into my own storehouses the things owed to be rendered to God. Then teaching something about the same the apostle says: If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it a great thing… and what follows.

For if I proclaim the gospel, it is no ground for me to boast; for necessity is laid upon me; and woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship (1 Corinthians 9:16–17). We are taught that whatever we do from necessity has no boast; but whatever we do by choice, with no necessity laid on, these things have a boast. For example: the one who does not commit adultery or murder does not have a boast, but the one who lives as a virgin; for he did not come to virginity from necessity but from choice. And where "woe" stands beside if I do not do it, I have no boast. Therefore he says: If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship. Again we are taught something catholic. Some things we do willingly with the whole soul; some things we do, yet not willingly nor with the whole soul, but from grief or from necessity. Of the things done by us willingly there is a reward; of the things done, yet as from grief, there is neither reward nor punishment. For example: I give alms; if willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I am not charged with those who hear: I was hungry and you did not give me to eat, and what follows (Matthew 25:42). This then is the reward: that where I have authority I may not do it.

For though I am free from all, I enslaved myself to all, that I might gain the more; and I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those under the law as under the law—though not myself under the law—that I might gain those under the law; to those without law as without law—not being without law toward God but under Christ's law—that I might gain those without law; I became to the weak as weak, that I might gain the weak; I have become all things to all, that by all means I might save some. And I do all things for the sake of the gospel, that I may become a fellow-sharer in it (1 Corinthians 9:19–23). To be free from all is of a perfect apostle. For someone can be free from fornication but a slave of anger, free from love of money but a slave of empty glory; he can be free from one sin but a slave of another. But to say "being free from all" is of a perfect apostle—such as Paul was. And according to what is before us the sense is such: I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews—for being free from Judaism I enslaved myself to Jews, that I might gain Jews; being free from being under the law I made myself as under the law, that I might gain those under the law. For Paul would go down into synagogues of Jews, would go in to them, would do according to their customs without harm, not sharing their pretense but hunting some from them. Some have asked what the difference is of those under the law beside the Jews; we say then that those under the law are other than Jews, as Samaritans. To those without law as without law: he came to Athens; he found philosophers there; he used not prophetic words nor legal ones, but wherever there was a lesson from Greek preparatory education he, recalling it, spoke to Athenians; for he says: as also some of your own poets have said, for we too are his offspring (Acts 17:28). There to those without law he became as without law, that he might gain those without law. And again he says: going through and observing your objects of worship, I found also an altar on which was inscribed: To an unknown god. What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I proclaim to you (Acts 17:23). And through these he begins to hand on reverence for God. english: —the lawless. At the same time he keeps his own exactness. “I became to the Jews as a Jew”: he did not say here, “not being a Jew.” For he was a Jew in secret, no longer in the open. And again: “to those under law as under law, though not myself under law”—here he had to put “not myself under law,” for [[Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law >> Bible:Galatians 3:13]], becoming a curse for us; as if he said, “not being a Samaritan.” “To the lawless as lawless, not being lawless toward God.” Someone will suppose I have become an apostate from the law and lawless toward God; I say that even if I do not keep the law according to the letter, I am not lawless toward God but under Christ’s law, keeping the polity according to the gospel, that I may win the lawless.

“I became to the weak as weak”: he did not say here “not myself being weak.” For it would have been boastful and arrogant, and not according to the apostle, to say “not myself being weak,” when he had heard from the Lord that [[my power is perfected in weakness >> Bible:2 Corinthians 12:9]] and for that reason boasts in weaknesses. How then was he weak to the weak? When he permits those who burn to marry; when he sympathizes with women who have lost husbands; when he says, [[because of porneias let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband >> Bible:1 Corinthians 7:2]], and the rest. In these he became weak to the weak, that he might win the weak. Then after this he says, “I have become all things to all, that I may save all or some.” Whichever person you take, he is one of the five: either Jew, or under law, or lawless, or weak, or “all.” The perfect is all; so to all—that is, to the perfect—I have become perfect, that I may win all. For he says, [[we speak wisdom among the perfect >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:6]], and what follows. This one can say, “I am a debtor both to Greeks and barbarians, both to wise and to unwise.”

[Origen:] Only the perfect can utter the perfect apostle’s word in the Lord: “I do all things for the sake of the gospel.” The one who sins cannot say this. If the one who does all for the gospel is a partner of the gospel, the one who commits porneia is a partner of the porneia of the spirit—and likewise with the other passions. Each becomes partner of that with which he shared. But someone among the hearers will say, “My life is mixed: I do not do all for the gospel, nor all for sin and pleasure.” To this we will say: God has these judgments; according to his many and varied judgments he repays.

44 on [[1 Corinthians 9:24 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 9:24]]: “Do you not know that those who run in a stadium all run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain.” [Origen:] Then do we all run and one receives the prize, and the rest perish? For he said one receives the prize while many run. All who are being saved are one and one body; for if we all share one bread and the same bread, we are all Christ’s body. So all the saved are the one who receives the prize. In the stadium, then, all run who order their life by a doctrine—those from the heresies who live by a doctrine, and perhaps Jews, and those who live by Greek doctrines while philosophizing. These are all who run in the stadium; the church also runs; but one receives the prize—the one man of whom the apostle says, [[until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ >> Bible:Ephesians 4:13]]. Yet every judgment of God must be found concerning all who run in the stadium, so that one may take first place and then each according to his worth.

45 on [[1 Corinthians 10:5 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 10:5]]: “But with most of them God was not well pleased, for they were struck down in the wilderness.” [Origen:] The apostle wants to show us that it is not merely obtaining a gift of God that saves the one who obtained it, but that after obtaining the gift one must remain, having become worthy of it. english: —the sons of Israel, though benefited so greatly, were not saved when they proved unworthy of God’s benefaction. For [[God was not well pleased with most of them >> Bible:1 Corinthians 10:5]]; they were struck down in the wilderness. And since the sinners were more and the righteous fewer, for that reason God was not well pleased with the many sinners rather than with the few righteous.

46 on [[1 Corinthians 10:6 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 10:6]]: “These things became types for us, so that we should not be desirers of evils, as they also desired.” [Origen:] He says these things have become types for us, so that we should not be desirers of evils as they desired. Those things were written typologically with a view to us, so that when we read the sins for which they suffered these things, we may keep ourselves from falling into the same desires as theirs.

47 on [[1 Corinthians 12:3 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:3]]: “Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says ‘Jesus is anathema,’ and no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except in the Holy Spirit.” [Origen:] There are many differences among spirits, which no one will know accurately unless he has the gift of discernment of spirits. And so that we may not too rashly either reject the spirits in those who speak or approve them, John says in the letter, [[Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are of God; every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in flesh is of God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not of God >> Bible:1 John 4:1-3]]. He also teaches us that when we hear people speaking we should neither assent at random nor rashly deny that what is said is from a divine spirit, but that each hearer, knowing he risks in the very act of approving or rejecting, should attend carefully neither to trust the false nor to distrust the true.

About this the apostle also adds next: [[If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I write is of God; but if anyone is ignorant, he is ignored >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:37-38]]. So not only is the one who ignores the apostle’s things ignored by God, but if someone ignores while speaking by a divine spirit—and were to say that he does not speak by a divine spirit—he is ignored by God. Through these things the apostle seems to teach that there is no human who does not have another spirit in him besides the spirit of the human that is in him. Whether he is alien to the faith or belonging to it, he has a spirit belonging to him from God.

How do we who hear the divine word need to learn that no one speaking in God’s Spirit says “Jesus is anathema”? Let us see: some can be ambiguous to those who do not know the facts accurately—whether they speak by God’s Spirit or not—while they anathematize Jesus. If ever you see a Jew expounding the divine Scriptures and not contemptibly, to the many, prophetic words, you might perhaps be in doubt whether God’s Spirit is also in that one. So that you may not be pulled about over such a person—whether a holy spirit is in him or not—Paul teaches that since every Jew says Jesus is anathema, and no one speaking in God’s Spirit says Jesus is anathema, the one who claims to know the law and the prophets while anathematizing Jesus does not have God’s Spirit. There is a heresy that does not receive the one who approaches unless he anathematize Jesus. And that heresy is worthy of the name it loved; for it is the heresy of the so-called Ophites, who say unlawful things in praise of the serpent, which is cursed by God.

He will call the more catholic sort, imitating the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah, second rank after the apostleship; but this last-ranked sort after the gifts already named is such as: [[if you prophesy, and an unbeliever or ungifted person comes in, he is convicted by all, examined by all, the secrets of his heart become plain, and so falling on his face he will worship God and announce that God is truly among you >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:24-25]]. For this is not far from the working of powers and the gift of healings that happen for the amazement of those who see, so that the one prophesying may say, “You have this in your heart; from this sin you have come to the church.” This prophecy can also be later in rank than the former ones, while that more divine and greater one is second, of which he says, [[God set in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:28]].

To establish that two things are signified from the name “prophecy,” I set out beforehand what I said. See whether I can still show the saying more clearly: God set in the church first apostles—but not all are apostles; for if all were apostles, to whom would they minister the apostleship? Second, prophets—not all are prophets; yet according to the other prophecy, “if you all prophesy, and an unbeliever or ungifted person comes in,” it is spoken not as of an impossibility but as of a possibility that all prophesy in that way. So there are two significations from the name “prophecy.” Therefore here too the apostle’s order is kept that says first apostles, second prophets, and the rest. So much concerning the order, since the phrase “to another prophecy,” ranked last in another wording, seemed to press us.

49 on [[1 Corinthians 13:1–2 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:1-2]]: “And I show you a still more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of humans and of angels, but do not have love, I have become a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.” [Origen:] We ask here whether someone in this life can both have prophecy and know all the mysteries without love, and altogether whether it is given to anyone to know all mysteries; for Paul says, [[If anyone thinks he has come to know something, he does not yet know as he ought to know >> Bible:1 Corinthians 8:2]]; and again, [[we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:9-10]]. Saying these things about himself and the apostles like him shows that it is not possible to know all mysteries and all knowledge. How then does he speak as if it were possible to know all knowledge and understand all mysteries?

If we look at the preface of the words, in which he says, “And I show you a still more excellent way,” and understand what “excellence” (hyperbole) is, all this will be clarified. Hyperbole, then, as even the Greeks defined it, is speech that for the sake of emphasis overshoots the truth; and they use the example that some are said to be whiter than snow—not that anything can be whiter than snow, but it is said by hyperbole. And again: some horses run like wind—not that such a thing is possible, but for emphasis, so that the horses’ speed may be shown, such a thing is said of them. And in the Scripture of the Psalms it is said of the sea, [[their waves go up to the heavens and go down to the abysses >> Bible:Psalm 107:26]]—which is impossible, but said for emphasis. And in the law you will find the manner of hyperbole written where it is written, [[We saw cities great and walled up to heaven >> Bible:Deuteronomy 1:28]]. How can this be? Yet it is said hyperbolically, the speech not altogether presenting the thing signified itself but showing the greatness of the waves or the lowliness, and the greatness of the walls, or something near these.

So also here the apostle takes a hypothesis in order that the nature of gifts and the nature of love may be examined—not that it is possible for a gift, and so great a gift, to exist without love; or that it is possible in this life for someone to know all knowledge without love, or to have such faith as to move mountains; but wanting to show that if love were set in a balance—the word being spoken by hypothesis. english: —conversing with one another—do they converse in these same tongues humans use, so that some angels would happen to be Greek, some Hebrew, others Egyptian? Or is it absurd to say this about the upper angelic ranks? Then perhaps, just as there are many dialects among humans, so also among angels? And if God grants us to be ranked from human nature into the angelic—my Lord Jesus Christ promising that [[they will be as angels and sons of God, being sons of the resurrection >> Bible:Luke 20:36]]—will we no longer use a human dialect but the angelic dialect? And just as children’s dialect differs from that of those whose voice is clear, so every human dialect is somehow a children’s dialect, while the angelic is somehow that of perfect and clear-voiced men? And perhaps there too, according to the analogy of their station, there are dialects. “If then I speak with the tongues of humans and of angels, but do not have love, I have become a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.” Just as sounding bronze gives an indistinct voice, and the clanging cymbal nothing clear, in the same way, without love, a tongue—even of angels among humans by hypothesis—is unclear; for nothing makes human or angelic speech clear and plain as love does; when love is absent, what is spoken is nothing.

What is the difference between knowledge and knowing the mysteries? For the apostle speaks about two things. I hold, then, that knowing about the open things is knowledge, more generic than the mysteries; for within a part of knowledge lies the science of the mysteries. But knowing about the more unspeakable and more divine things is knowing the mystery—so that there is a generic account of knowledge, yet not every grasp of knowledge is grasp of mysteries, about which it is said, [[But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:7]]. When I know these things, then I have the knowledge of the mysteries. “And if I have all faith so as to move mountains”: it is written in the gospel, [[If you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you >> Bible:Matthew 17:20]]. For the one who has faith as a mustard seed has the whole of faith.

50 on [[1 Corinthians 13:3 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:3]]: “And if I give away all my possessions as food, and if I hand over my body that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing.” [Origen:] “If I feed people with all my goods” not because of love; “if I hand over my body that I may boast”—as if it were possible to give away goods not for love but for empty glory, and as if it were possible also to bear witness for the sake of boasting and the glory with which martyrs are glorified in the churches.

51 on [[1 Corinthians 13:4–5 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:4-5]]: “Love is patient, is kind; love does not envy; love does not brag, is not puffed up, does not behave indecently, does not seek its own.” [Origen:] He goes through the praises of the love that surpasses the gifts. For he had to teach both what love is and how the one who has love is. “Love is patient”: if you have patience that is a fruit of the Spirit, you have it because of love. “Is kind”: what is opposite to kindness? Wickedness. If you act wickedly against anyone, you do not have love. If you are kind and sweet toward all humans, you have love. “Love does not envy”: if there is envy in you like Cain’s toward Abel or like Joseph’s brothers toward Joseph, you do not have love. Loving and envying are fighting things. “Love does not brag”: when someone is rash, professing to know about a craft or a science or knowledge, that one is the braggart because he does not have love. “Does not behave indecently”: no one who has love does anything indecent; so if ever a brother and sister claiming to love one another according to God fall through weakness under the pretext of love, let us tell them they do not have love; for love does not behave indecently. “Does not seek its own”: no one who has love seeks his own things; for example a mother loving her son, or a father, does not seek his own as he seeks the son’s; for having love is not self-loving. If the Savior, being in the form of God and equal with God, had sought his own, he would have remained in that form; but now, wanting to save a perishing world, [[he emptied himself, taking a slave’s form >> Bible:Philippians 2:6-8]]; and being found in fashion as a human he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto—

english: of death, even death on a cross. Come also to the saints; see Moses’ love: [[If you forgive them their sin, forgive; if not, blot me out of your book which you have written >> Bible:Exodus 32:32]]. And the apostle also says, [[just as I also please all in all things, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many, that they may be saved >> Bible:1 Corinthians 10:33]], and [[I could wish to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh >> Bible:Romans 9:3]]. He prays to be anathema from Christ for the salvation of others.
52 on [[1 Corinthians 13:8 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:8]]: “Whether tongues, they will cease.” [Origen:] Tongues will cease when I converse with mind to the one with whom I wish to speak.

53 on [[1 Corinthians 13:9–12 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:9-12]]: “For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, then the partial will be done away. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, thought as a child, reasoned as a child; when I became a man, I did away with the things of the child. For now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face.” [Origen:] The one who seems to advance here advances as among children; but when the perfect comes and we attain to a perfect man, then we will contain the things of men—knowledge and prophecy and the vision of God which the blessed will see because of purity of heart.

54 on [[1 Corinthians 14:5 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:5]]: “For the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the church may receive building.” [Origen:] The one who has the building gift is greater than the one who does not, inasmuch as the one with the building gift is more useful to the common good; but if the one speaking in tongues also has interpretation for building the church, the prophet is no longer greater. For sometimes he speaks high things, speaking to himself and to God, so that the church cannot hear.

55 on [[1 Corinthians 14:6 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:6]]: “But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you unless I speak to you either in revelation or in prophecy or in knowledge or in teaching?” [Origen:] Prophecy is knowledge that signifies the unseen through speech—knowledge of the world’s constitution and of the working of elements and times. Teaching is the instructional word distributed to the many. Revelation is when the mind goes outside earthly things and puts away every fleshly practice by God’s power; the one who obtains this has come into revelation. Perhaps also knowledge about future things can be called revelation; and one who has understood each term’s proper sense may use the names more loosely.

56 on [[1 Corinthians 14:7–9a >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:7-9]]: lifeless flute or lyre without distinction of notes; trumpet without clear call; tongues without clear speech. [Origen:] He wants to shame those who speak in a tongue into silence in church if there is no interpreter. Lifeless flute and lyre that give no distinction of musical notes are not known by what rhythm they played; the soldier does not arm for war unless the trumpet utters the voice that rouses to war; and those who speak in a tongue and do not interpret ought not to speak, as giving no distinction to the words for understanding. He called the doctrines of contemplation flute and lyre as showing nothing ethical, and those who urge toward virtue a trumpet. Hence one may say that the unclear parts of Scripture—such as the sacrifices in Leviticus and the tent in Exodus—should not be read unless someone clarifies their mind by exposition.

57 on [[1 Corinthians 14:9b >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:9]]: “For you will be speaking into the air.” [Origen:] The one who speaks in a tongue speaks in God; even if humans do not understand, still the powers about the air hear.
58 on [[1 Corinthians 14:10 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:10]]: “There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is voiceless.”

english: [Origen:] So even the lifeless give voice, some with this distinction of notes, some without it; for every body has a property of voice when it strikes another body.

59 on [[1 Corinthians 14:11 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:11]]: “If then I do not know the force of the voice, I will be a barbarian to the speaker and the speaker a barbarian in me.” [Origen:] Everyone who speaks to someone what that one does not understand seems a barbarian to the hearer, and that one to him.

60 on [[1 Corinthians 14:12 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:12]]: “So also you, since you are zealots for spirits, seek to abound toward the building of the church.” [Origen:] Abounding happens by the superiority of gifts from seeking what builds the church, inasmuch as the one who does not seek the common good does not abound in the gifts. For likely the working of the gift is idle when it does not shine before humans. Therefore if we want the gifts to grow, we will give ourselves over to the benefit of the many.

61 on [[1 Corinthians 14:13–14 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:13-14]]: “Therefore let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.” [Origen:] If the tongue speaker does not have the gift of interpreting, even if others do not understand, he himself understands what is cast into him from the spirit so that he is moved to speak. But when what is spoken is understood by others, then that seems to be fruit of the speaker toward those who understand.

62 on [[1 Corinthians 14:15–17 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:15-17]]: pray and sing with spirit and mind; otherwise the ungifted cannot say Amen and is not built. [Origen:] Through these too we are taught to seek the common good of the church.

63 on [[1 Corinthians 14:18–19 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:18-19]]: “I thank my God, speaking in tongues more than you all; but in church I want to speak five words with my mind, that I may also catechize others, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue.” [Origen:] Even speaking the sense words spiritually is seeking the common good of the five senses; and the word of catechesis through the five senses is set for the hearers in church, as they too are catechized by the five words. For those who do not know the clarity of what is said, but attend only to the bare sound of the Scriptures, are called catechumens; but those who hear the distinction of the notes from Scripture are not catechumens but faithful.

64 on [[1 Corinthians 14:20 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:20]]: “Brothers, do not be children in your minds, but be infants in evil, and in your minds become perfect.” [Origen:] Since what he commands is possible, it is possible for us to become perfect in our minds. This nearly interprets, [[Unless you turn and become as the children >> Bible:Matthew 18:3]]; for the one who is an infant in evil, having turned, becomes as a child.

65 on [[1 Corinthians 14:21 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:21]]: “In the law it is written, ‘In other tongues and with other lips I will speak to this people, and not even so will they hear me, says the Lord.’” [Origen:] He also called the prophetic word “law”; and we found these words in Aquila and the other editions, not indeed in the Seventy.

66 on [[1 Corinthians 14:24–25 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:24-25]]: if all prophesy, the unbeliever is convicted, heart secrets laid bare, and he falls and worships, announcing God is truly among you. [Origen:] Since the prophetic gift makes known the secrets of the unbeliever’s and ungifted person’s heart when he draws near them, clearly when the perfect comes they will know perfectly every ungifted and unbeliever’s secrets—and likely then also the holy person’s secrets become plain to the prophets, perhaps the greater knowing the lesser’s. And the one benefited is cautious to look into God’s face; therefore imagining God he falls on his face, giving him the superiority and glory, and so worships God. Convicting and examining the heart’s secrets—that is, making them plain—marks that God is in the spirit of such people. And if the other gifts too are signs that God truly is, in what must one seek?

english: interpret. [Origen:] When we come together, all who have gifts and are able to teach must be allowed to speak.

68 on [[1 Corinthians 14:29 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:29]]: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others discern.” [Origen:] By “others” he means those who have the gift of clarifying the prophets’ spiritual words, if indeed the prophesying ones themselves did not have the gift of discernment; for in what they lack this, they may well have been deceived by some wicked spirit transforming itself into an angel of light, as if they had obtained prophetic rank.

69 on [[1 Corinthians 14:30–31 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:30-31]]: “If a revelation is made to another sitting by, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one.” [Origen:] Therefore the prophets were not beside themselves; for in them was the power to be silent and to hold back the spirit upon them.

70 on [[1 Corinthians 14:32 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:32]]: “And spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.” [Origen:] For this reason the subjection shows willingly in silence; that the spirits are subject to the prophets, but it is the prophets’ souls that prophesy.

71 on [[1 Corinthians 14:34–35 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:34-35]]: “Let your women be silent in the churches; for it is not permitted them to speak, but to be subject, as also the law says. If they wish to learn something, let them ask their own husbands at home.” [Origen:] Since from the beginning the men had authority to speak and benefit the hearers, and the women asked about what they were unsure of. And by “law” he means what is said in Genesis, [[Your turning shall be to your husband >> Bible:Genesis 3:16]].

72 on [[1 Corinthians 14:37–38 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:37-38]]: “If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I write to you are the Lord’s commandments; but if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant.” [Origen:] Spiritual is the one able to test every word and every mind, and through great depth of mind hard to diagnose so as not to be examined. It is not for just anyone to know that what Paul writes is the Lord’s, but for a prophet or spiritual; therefore the one who does not know it is the Lord’s is neither prophet nor spiritual. Believing is one thing and knowing another; therefore the one ignorant that it is the Lord’s is ignorant, not yet having arrived at truly being God’s; for the one known is somehow mixed into the one who knows him.

73 on [[1 Corinthians 14:31 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:31]]: “For you can all prophesy one by one, that all may learn and all be encouraged.” [Origen:] There is danger for those who read to declare simply, and likewise for those who hear. Hear Paul saying, [[If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual among you, let him acknowledge that what I write is of God >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:37]], as if not everyone knows the things of God unless he is prophet or spiritual. And the apostle sketched the spiritual when he said, [[The spiritual examines all things, yet he himself is examined by no one >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:15]]. Who is the one discerning all things but the one able to scrutinize and judge every word? And he is examined by no one, because the depth of his thoughts is not grasped. For the spiritual has the mind of the Lord. Just as a child cannot examine a man’s mind and scrutinize his thoughts—for the small child does not even follow a man’s thoughts at the start—so neither can the soulish know which things are God’s and which are not; this work belongs only to the spiritual.

I often asked myself why, when there were God’s prophets and false prophets, the false prophets were in favor with their kings more than the prophets; and the false prophets’ books were not written or preserved among the people, while the books of the prophets who were condemned, hated, and suffered what we know came into the open and are honored. What was the beginning of this? Taking cues from the apostle I say: there was a gift among the people, as of prophesying, so also of discerning prophets. “For you can all prophesy one by one”: there was then abundance of speakers and of those permitted to speak. For this reason the apostle allowed all to speak in church; he almost allowed even the women to speak, if he had not said what follows.

74 on [[1 Corinthians 14:34–35 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:34-35]] again: women silent in churches; ask husbands at home; shameful for women to speak in church. [Origen:] As if all speak and can speak when a revelation comes to them, he says women are to be silent in the churches. english: husband of the bride. But still let us be fair and meet even their plausible points. They say Philip the evangelist had four daughters and they prophesied. If they prophesied, what is absurd, as those people say, if our women also prophesy as prophetesses? We will solve this. First by saying: our women prophesied—show the signs of prophecy in them. Second: even if Philip’s daughters prophesied, they did not speak in the churches; for we do not have this in the Acts of the Apostles. Nor in the old: Deborah is attested a prophetess, and Miriam sister of Aaron took the tambourine and led the women. But you would not find that Deborah harangued the people like Jeremiah and Isaiah; you would not find that Huldah, being a prophetess, spoke to the people but to one who came to her. And in the gospel Anna is recorded a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel of Asher’s tribe; but she did not speak in church. So even if a woman is granted to be a prophetess from a prophetic sign, she is still not permitted to speak in church. When Miriam the prophetess spoke she was leader of certain women; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church, and [[I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man >> Bible:1 Timothy 2:12]].

I will also show this from elsewhere, even if that was said more securely about the woman not becoming leader by the man’s word: [[an older woman in a deportment sacred, a good teacher, that she may train the young women >> Bible:Titus 2:3-4]]—not simply that they teach. For let women also be good teachers, not so that men sit and hear women as if men able to ambassad God’s word were lacking. “If they wish to learn something, let them ask their own husbands at home; for it is shameful for women to speak in church.” It seems to me “their own husbands” does not refer only to married men; for virgins would either speak in church or have no teachers, and widows likewise; but perhaps “own men” such as brother and household member and son? Once for all let a woman inquire of her own man according to the generic name “man” over against “woman”; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church, whatever she may say, even if she says wonders, even if holy things, only because it comes from a woman’s mouth. “Woman in church” is clearly said under the shameful for accusation of the whole church.

[[1 Corinthians 14:36 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:36]]: “Or did the word of God go out from you, or did it come to you alone?” As if this disorder was in Corinth along with the other sins. So he says God sent his word into the world. Did the truth and the church rule then come only to you Corinthians?

75 on [[1 Corinthians 14:37–38 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:37-38]]: acknowledge what I write are the Lord’s commands; if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant. [Origen:] So that we may know the things of God, let us ask the Giver of gifts to give us a prophetic gift and make us spiritual from the ruling spirit; and so be ready to judge which things are God’s and which are not. For the one deprived of this grace cannot understand; hence he added, “If anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant.”

76 on [[1 Corinthians 15:1–2 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:1-2]]: “I make known to you, brothers, the gospel which I gospelled to you, which also you received, in which also you stand, through which also you are saved, by what word I gospelled to you, if you hold it fast—unless you believed in vain.” [Origen:] He calls gospel what he gospels, for this he also handed on; and this one stands in the gospel who has his soul mounted on it as on a boat, through which he is also saved. And he says the one who does not hold the gospel’s word has believed in vain—having heard irrationally and by chance and not by examination. [Origen:] Jews have not stood in the gospel, not receiving Jesus; those from the heresies stand badly, not understanding the gospel but taking it in their own way; those who sin have not stood, not living according to the gospel. Who then have stood in the gospel but those who received it and accepted it and live according to it? And if “by what word I gospelled to you, if you hold fast” is understood, and the following “unless you believed in vain” is understood reasonably with these, we will know that it is impossible for the one who believed in vain thus—

english: —believed a falsehood; but to have believed what is true is not yet a work; belief is in judgment. Those who believe before the time and fall away in a time of trial believe in vain; and yet they have not believed false things but the true—yet because they have not believed firmly, for that reason they fall away in a time of trial. For one who believes well will not fall.

77 on [[1 Corinthians 15:5 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:5]]: “And that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve.” [Origen:] He says the Lord appeared to the Twelve after the resurrection; for it is likely that Matthias also was present, who was set as apostle in Judas’s place.

78 on [[1 Corinthians 15:9 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:9]]: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not fit to be called apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.” [Origen:] Conscious of the sins from which he was freed, he says, “I am not fit to be called apostle.”

79 on [[1 Corinthians 15:10 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:10]]: “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than they all—yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” [Origen:] Having said that his grace toward me was not empty, he taught that those who live unworthily of the grace received it empty. It is not that grace labors, but it must be understood thus: “I did not do these things, but the grace that is with me.”

80 on [[1 Corinthians 15:11 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:11]]: “Whether then I or they, so we preach and so you believed.” [Origen:] All the apostles having been fully persuaded about Christ’s resurrection from the dead, the proof is firm; therefore we say the same things; for you also believed thus.

81 on [[1 Corinthians 15:12–13 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:12-13]]: if Christ is preached raised, how do some say there is no resurrection of the dead? [Origen:] Christ’s resurrection with the flesh he had is clear from the text before us. But some, or rather the heterodox, want to allegorize humans’ resurrection; let them allegorize the Savior’s too, badly rejecting the wording. [[He means Manicheans who say that the one freed from sins thus rose from the dead.]]

82 on [[1 Corinthians 15:14 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:14]]: “If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty.” [Origen:] Since neither the preaching nor the faith is empty, it is clear Christ has been raised. We noted these things to show that even if Paul knew dialectical arguments, he used them naturally; for from nature and custom the dialectical art was embodied by those who philosophize.

83 on [[1 Corinthians 15:15–16 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:15-16]]: false witnesses of God if the dead are not raised. [Origen:] If the one who says Christ rose bears false witness against God, then also everyone who says there is a resurrection of the dead; but if Christ rose as firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, it is clear the dead are raised.

84 on [[1 Corinthians 15:20–23 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:20-23]]: Christ raised as firstfruits; through a human death and resurrection; in Adam all die, in Christ all made alive; each in his own order. [Origen:] Since those from the heresies who say the church faith and sneer at it as faith of fools reject in deed, if not in word, that resurrection happens as the church believes—see how one must meet them from this apostolic wording and from countless others. Did Christ rise from the dead, or not? But every heresy has agreed about this. If Christ rose from the dead, and he is firstborn from the dead, and no one is firstborn of another kind, his resurrection must be of the same kind as the resurrection of those who rise. For example: Reuben is firstborn, being a son of Jacob—
